Key Takeaways
  • A structured EDR alert checklist helps analysts review critical evidence consistently and reduce investigation gaps.
  • Investigations should cover endpoints, users, files, processes, file modification times, and process hierarchies.
  • The analyst must confirm the alerts as true or false positives, and rank them according to asset criticality, user privilege and business impact.
  • By tracing the execution, follow-on activity, persistence, network connections and initial access vector, it can be determined what the total attack path and scope was.
  • Correlating EDR with other security data and taking containment, eradication, and response actions enables faster and more confident incident handling.

Security teams don’t usually struggle when it comes to EDR alerts; they struggle when it comes to details about the critical investigation that are spread across alerts, endpoint telemetry, user activity, process trees and threat intelligence.

When an alert comes in, it could be a sign of something suspicious, and the analysts must be fast to determine what, how, where and whether or not the threat has stepped beyond its original endpoint.

An organized list of EDR alerts aids analysts during triage and investigation to focus on the most important evidence. This data can help expedite investigations and aid in decision making for response. Process activity, user activity, command-line activity, persistence mechanisms and indicators of compromise (IOCs) are all key details that can be included.

Security teams can use this checklist to help determine the next actions to take, and the level of severity and scope of the alert when reviewing any EDR alert.

EDR Alert Checklist
1. Classify the Alert

Before you investigate the alert, you need to learn what caused the alert and what kind of activity the alert is alerting you to. Knowing the problem gives analysts the ability to know which path to take in an investigation and not waste time on non-telemetry.

  • Identify whether the alert is file, process, network, or asset-based.
  • Identify the exact detection of trigger, rule, or behavioral signal.
  • Review the alert severity and confidence score.
  • Record the affected endpoint, user, and timestamp.
  • Determine whether similar alerts exist elsewhere.
Fidelis Endpoint®: A Technical Deep Dive
  • How Fidelis Prevent, Detect, and Respond
  • Threat Prevention and Intelligence
  • Investigating, Hunting, and Forensics
Read Technical Brief
2. Establish the Alert Context

An alert usually only gives insufficient information. Construct the context around the event in relation to the endpoint, file, process and activity just prior to and following the detection.

  • Record the hostname, IP address, operating system, and endpoint type.
  • Identify the logged-in user and privilege level.
  • Capture the relevant file hash, filename, and file path.
  • Record file creation, modification, and execution timestamps.
  • Identify any process created or launched by the suspicious file, and any files it downloaded.
  • Review the parent-child process hierarchy.
3. Determine Whether It Is a True Positive

Prior to escalating an alert, consider whether malicious activity was detected or not. Use a combination of reputation, behavioral evidence, user context, and historical activity, not just one of these factors.

  • Check the file, domain, IP, or other indicator against threat intelligence.
  • Review the detection's confidence and supporting evidence.
  • Determine whether the activity is expected for the application or user.
  • Search for the same indicator across the environment.
  • Classify the alert as a true positive, false positive, or inconclusive.
  • Document the evidence supporting the verdict.
4. Check Existing Containment and Remediation

EDR platforms may already have taken automated action before an analyst begins the investigation. Confirm what happened and whether those actions actually removed the threat.

  • Check whether the suspicious file was quarantined or deleted.
  • Confirm whether the endpoint was isolated.
  • Verify that automated remediation is completed successfully.
  • Review any failed or partially completed response actions.
  • Determine whether additional containment is necessary.
  • Record all automated and analyst-initiated actions.
5. Prioritize Based on Risk and Impact

The same alert can represent very different levels of risk depending on the affected asset and user. Use business context to determine how urgently the alert needs to be investigated and contained.

  • Assess the criticality of the affected endpoint.
  • Determine the user's role and privilege level.
  • Check access to sensitive systems or data.
  • Identify whether privileged or high-value accounts are involved.
  • Consider the potential business impact of compromise.
  • Escalate high-risk alerts for immediate investigation or containment.
6. Confirm Whether the Threat Executed

A suspicious file being present on an endpoint does not necessarily mean it is executed. Establish whether execution occurred and identify exactly what happened afterward.

  • Confirm whether the suspicious file or binary is executed.
  • Review process creation telemetry.
  • Identify the parent process and execution chain.
  • Review command-line arguments.
  • Establish the execution timeline.
  • Check for evidence of malicious behavior following execution.
7. Investigate Follow-On Activity

If execution occurs, investigate what the process did next. Follow-on activity can reveal payload delivery, persistence, credential access, lateral movement, or command-and-control behavior.

  • Trace the complete process tree.
  • Identify files created, modified, or downloaded.
  • Check for persistence mechanisms and registry changes.
  • Review suspicious child processes and process injection activity.
  • Investigate outbound network connections.
  • Identify additional payloads or attack stages.
  • Determine whether the endpoint remains compromised.
8. Trace the Origin of the Activity

Once the immediate activity is understood, work backward to determine how it reached the endpoint. Finding the origin helps identify the initial access vector and prevent recurrence.

  • Work backward from the file or process creation timestamp.
  • Review activity immediately preceding the detection.
  • Check browser, web, and network activity.
  • Determine whether a suspicious URL, download, attachment, or application is involved.
  • Identify the mechanism that introduced the file or payload.
  • Establish the most likely initial access vector.
9. Correlate EDR With Other Security Data

Endpoint telemetry often provides only one part of the attack story. Correlating EDR data with identity, email, cloud, network, and SIEM telemetry can reveal how the activity started and whether it spreads.

  • Pivot from the endpoint to relevant identity and cloud logs.
  • Correlate events using the affected user and timestamps.
  • Review email activity when phishing is suspected.
  • Identify suspicious senders, URLs, attachments, or cloud events.
  • Search for related indicators across other security platforms.
  • Determine whether other users or endpoints were exposed.
10. Contain, Eradicate, and Scope the Threat

The last step removing a single malicious file. Security teams should strive to contain the immediate threat, determine the extent of exposure, remove persistence, and ensure the attacker no longer has access.

  • Isolate compromised endpoints where necessary.
  • Terminate malicious processes and remove malicious files.
  • Remove persistence mechanisms and unauthorized changes.
  • Block malicious hashes, domains, IPs, URLs, or senders.
  • Search for the same indicators across the organization.
  • Identify and remediate additional affected endpoints or accounts.
  • Reset compromised credentials where required.
  • Confirm that malicious activity has stopped.
  • Document the timeline, evidence, findings, and response actions.
How Fidelis Endpoint Helps After an Attack

  • Rapid Threat Hunting:

  • Built-in Response Orchestration:

Fidelis Endpoint® also supports remote investigations, endpoint isolation, quarantine of suspicious data, and automated response actions without requiring analysts to switch between multiple tools. items.title: Fast-Track Your PQC Strategy: A Template for OMB M-26-15 Readiness
items.summary: Your Template for OMB M-26-15 Migration The transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is not just a technical upgrade; it is a vital national security imperative that represents the most significant cryptographic reset in the history of the Federal Government. Driven by Executive Order 14412 and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) M-26-15 , Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies face a strict October 22, 2026 deadline to submit comprehensive PQC Migration Plans to OMB and the Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD). To take the heavy lifting off agency leaders facing this tight 120-day window, we developed a ready-to-use Template for OMB M-26-15 Readiness and OMB M-26-15 PQC Migration Plan Instructions . Precision-engineered to align directly with the White House mandates, this template serves as a "fast-track" for federal teams. Instead of spending limited cycles building complex compliance documentation from scratch, security leaders can leverage this template to rapidly map their transition pathways and shift their focus to active discovery and remediation. Per M-26-15, each agency’s migration plan must contain, at a minimum, nine core elements, all of which are featured in the PQC Migration Plan Template: System prioritization strategy with risk-based justification. Timelines and milestones to achieve the first three migration phases. TLS 1.3 support milestones for the January 2, 2030, deadline. Methodologies and automated tools for cryptographic inventory. Cryptographic agile architecture implementation plan. Third-party coordination plan. Estimate of funding and personnel resources. Risk management strategy for the migration period. Governance roles and responsibilities definition. Agencies must specifically prioritize high impact systems, High Value Assets (HVAs), and any systems vulnerable to cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) based attacks. This includes logical access control systems based in asymmetric encryption (such as PKI) and any data expected to remain mission-sensitive through 2030. For most agencies, the core challenge of a migration plan is uncovering "cryptographic debt,” the years of hidden, legacy encryption buried in fractured IT systems. Because this debt creates unseen risks, establishing cryptographic visibility is the primary enabler for success. Once you can see your entire environment, the path to a quantum-safe future becomes clear and manageable. A successful migration plan depends on an agency's ability to move quickly and accurately, requiring a fundamental shift in security architecture that prioritizes active discovery over passive lists. By deploying a structured and automated methodology, agencies gain the real-time visibility necessary to: Discover their full cryptographic footprint with total clarity. Protect critical assets against immediate and emerging threats. Accelerate the rollout of quantum-safe resilience across the enterprise. To maximize your team’s resources, our OMB M-26-15 PQC Migration Plan Instructions and Template for OMB M-26-15 Readiness are a practical "fast-track" for building a compliant transition plan. This template provides a clear implementation methodology and a detailed checklist to ensure all required elements are addressed. I. Policy Foundation The federal mandate is driven by two specific directives that agencies must operationalize: Executive Order 14412: Accelerates the Federal Government's transition to post-quantum cryptography to mitigate emerging quantum computing threats. OMB Memorandum M-26-15: Directs each agency to prioritize critical information technology for migration and develop a plan that integrates PQC readiness into existing governance structures. While this specific policy targets federal agencies, the global trend is clear: critical infrastructure operators and private sector entities should view this mandate as a strategic blueprint. II. Compliance Timeline & Milestones M-26-15 establishes a multi-phased timeline for agency compliance. While initial efforts focus on prioritizing HVAs and high-impact systems to mitigate immediate risk, agencies are expected to complete migration across remaining systems by 2035. Deadline Policy Requirement & Milestone July 22, 2026 PQC Migration Lead Designation: Agencies must formally identify a PQC migration lead. Oct 22, 2026 Submittal of PQC Migration Plan: Deadline for agencies to deliver a dynamic migration roadmap to OMB and ONCD. Jan 2, 2030 TLS 1.3 Implementation: Agencies must support TLS 1.3 (or a successor version) to enable the extensible handshake needed for hybrid-PQC key exchange models. Dec 31, 2030 Key Establishment Deadline: Agencies must transition all HVAs and high impact systems to PQC (FIPS 203 ML-KEM) for key establishment. Dec 31, 2031 Digital Signature Deadline: Transition all HVAs and high impact systems to PQC for digital signatures using FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) or FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA). III. Mandatory Elements of the PQC Migration Plan Agency heads must ensure that their submitted plans address the following nine core elements: System Prioritization Strategy: Risk-based justification addressing HVAs and PKI-based logical access control systems. Timelines and Milestones: Phased migration plans within the initial planning horizon. TLS 1.3 Support Milestones: Testing and deployment timelines for the 2030 deadline. Methodologies and Automated Tools: Documentation of tools used for cryptographic inventory. Cryptographic Agile Architecture: Strategy for algorithm rotation via configuration rather than code. Third-Party Coordination Plan: Delineating the Shared Responsibility Model with cloud providers. Resource & Personnel Allocation: Estimates for annual budget requests. Risk Management Strategy: Specific to the migration period itself. Governance Roles and Responsibilities: Defining implementation and risk acceptance accountability. IV. Strategic Phasing: Multi-Year Transformation Discovery & Strategy (2026-2027): Inventory, assessment, and governance framework setup. Piloting (2027-2028): Early migration of prioritized systems. Prioritized Key Migration (2028-2030): HVAs and systems vulnerable to CRQC-based attacks. Signature Migration (2031): Digital signature protocols for prioritized systems. Full Enterprise Migration (2035): Completion for all remaining systems. V. Operationalizing the Transition with QSS Quantum-Safe Security (QSS) , a FedRAMP Moderate authorized tool , helps agencies move from box-checking to real operational resilience. Strategic alignment with M-26-15: Automated Discovery and CBOM Generation: Real-time visibility and generation of Cryptographic Bills of Materials (CBOM) to identify hidden dependencies. FedRAMP Authorized: Accelerates adoption by removing the need for a separate agency-level ATO for the discovery tool. Validation of Cryptographic Agility: Ensures systems can rotate to NIST standards (ML-KEM, ML-DSA) without hard-coded updates. Integration with Zero Trust: Secures the cryptographic roots of device attestation and inter-service communication. VI. Deploying, maintaining, and migrating production n8n on EKS
items.summary: n8n is easy to try and harder to run under production traffic. A single container with SQLite works great for a quick demo. Production is a different story entirely. You need workers, webhook processors, PostgreSQL, Redis, object storage, external secrets, ingress routing, and an upgrade plan that preserves workflow history. Engineering teams rely on n8n to connect internal systems, process webhooks, and automate critical business data pipelines. It is also showing up in AI workloads, including self-hosted agents and RAG pipelines. Those workloads can put more pressure on workers, secrets management, and state handling. We deployed n8n on Amazon EKS, ran it under real traffic, and later moved from a community Helm chart to n8n’s official Helm chart . The platform stayed in place, and we kept the database, queue, object storage, IAM role, and secrets intact through the cutover. Why we started with the community chart The community chart got us to production. It supported queue mode, additional ingress configuration, and StatefulSet-based main pods, which matched our architectural requirements at the time. We ran it for about a year. Over time, maintaining unsupported features and local patches became harder to justify. We compared the available options and decided to move to the official chart, where ongoing maintenance and active community support gave us a clearer path for future upgrades. How we ran n8n We ran n8n in queue mode on EKS. In queue mode, the main instance manages workflow information and triggers, while worker instances execute jobs from the Redis queue. Dedicated webhook processors handled production webhook traffic separately. We split ingress by traffic type. Public webhooks ran behind an internet-facing load balancer, while internal webhooks used a private hostname. That separation fit our traffic patterns. Workers handled workflow execution. PostgreSQL stored workflow and execution data, Redis handled queued jobs, and S3 stored binary files. Because licensing multi-replica main pods is an Enterprise capability, we needed a secure, consistent way to handle shared application configuration and encryption key secrets across pods. We stored those secrets in AWS Secrets Manager and synced them into Kubernetes using External Secrets Operator (ESO). This synchronized application credentials, API keys, and environment variables into Kubernetes Secrets. What changed with the official chart The community chart ran the main pod as a StatefulSet with one persistent volume per replica. Workers and webhook processors already ran as Deployments. That StatefulSet configuration avoided multi-attach issues on AWS gp3 ReadWriteOnce (RWO) EBS volumes when running more than one main pod. In our configuration, the official chart used a different workload model, with main running as a Deployment and persistence relying on a single shared PVC. Our gp3 volume could not attach to multiple main pods across nodes, so an in-place Helm upgrade did not fit the deployment. We treated the migration as a full cutover instead. The shared persistence requirement was our main design decision. We checked what was stored on disk before carrying it forward: PostgreSQL held workflow and execution data. Redis held queued jobs. S3 held files. AWS Secrets Manager held the encryption key and application secrets. We found nothing on the main pod volume that needed to persist. With PostgreSQL, Redis, S3, and Secrets Manager holding the required application state, a replacement main pod could start and reconnect without relying on a pod-specific disk. We disabled main persistence entirely for the official chart deployment. Moving traffic safely The platform stayed in place: we kept the database, object storage, IAM role, and secrets through the cutover. Everything else was recreated from the new chart values. Before the production migration, we: Tested rollback in a non-prod environment Took a database snapshot Saved secrets to a secondary location Did not change the n8n image version. A version bump could trigger a database migration, and we wanted to keep the database out of the cutover story We tested in non-production first with a restored database snapshot: pods healthy, known workflows completing, required endpoints reachable. We verified rollback there before touching live traffic. The Helm release changed. PostgreSQL, Redis, S3, IAM, and secrets stayed. For a public example of how we structure official-chart values for external Postgres/Redis, queue mode + HPA, resources, ingress/webhooks, optional task runners, see: github.com/husne-fairwinds/n8n-sample Fairwinds helps teams manage Kubernetes environments, with a focus on operational reliability, security, and maintainability.

Our gp3 volume could not attach to multiple main pods across nodes, so an in-place Helm upgrade did not fit the deployment. We treated the migration as a full cutover instead.

  • PostgreSQL held workflow and execution data.

items.title: Managing open-weight model risk in enterprise deployments
items.summary: The growing AI landscape is giving enterprises more choice in how they build, customize, and deploy increasingly capable models. Open-weight models are an important part of that landscape. They give enterprises access to model weights and greater flexibility to inspect, evaluate, modify, and run models within their own environments. While that flexibility can be valuable, it also affects how enterprises evaluate models, where they implement safeguards, and who is responsible for maintaining those safeguards over time. As enterprises choose which models to deploy, the relevant question is broader than whether a model is open-weight or closed-weight. Enterprises need to understand what they are using the model for, what could go wrong in that context, and what evidence and controls they need to manage risks. Today, Microsoft and NVIDIA are publishing Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise , the first in a planned series of joint resources intended to help enterprises address those questions. The paper introduces a shared risk taxonomy and an approach to managing model risks grounded in established standards and frameworks, including International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standards and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework. The paper reflects a core idea: weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk. Risk depends on the model, use case, deployment, and safeguards. Read the whitepaper: Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise Understanding risk in the deployment context Open- and closed-weight models can share many of the same underlying risks, but how those risks materialize depends on the deployment. A model used to help an employee draft a document presents different considerations than the same model used in a customer-facing workflow, just as a standalone inference endpoint differs from a system connected to external data or tools. The architecture matters too. A risk may originate in the model, while the most effective control may sit in the inference environment, application, or surrounding operational processes. The joint guidance looks beyond the model label to factors including provenance, intended use, users, deployment conditions, and surrounding controls. This first paper focuses primarily on model-layer risks. Evaluating a model alone does not establish the safety of an agent or application: teams must also assess its permissions, data access, tools, runtime, and operational controls. Establishing a common language Managing these risks consistently also requires a common vocabulary across engineering, security, legal, safety, and business teams. The initial Microsoft and NVIDIA taxonomy organizes risks into five broad categories: Cybersecurity, Data Protection, Content, Human-AI Interaction, and Bias. It is not a policy or deployment checklist, but instead it should be used by enterprises to adapt it to their own systems, use cases, and risk criteria, then connect relevant risks to evaluations, mitigations, and accountable owners. Using evaluations as risk evidence Evaluations help turn the taxonomy into something enterprises can use. The paper maps evaluations to a selection of risks across the five categories, giving teams a way to start with a risk that matters for their deployment and identify evaluations that can produce relevant evidence about it. Microsoft Foundry helps enterprises assess quality, groundedness, and safety with built-in and custom evaluations and automated red teaming. Its configurable content-safety controls help detect and mitigate harmful inputs and outputs and prompt attacks. Teams should validate control availability for their model and deployment, including preview status, and combine these capabilities with application-specific testing, monitoring, and human oversight. Evaluations still need to be interpreted in the context of a particular deployment and the goal is to make it easier for teams to connect the risks they identify with useful evidence, while building a broader set of evaluation resources that can evolve alongside models, deployment patterns, and emerging risks. Microsoft and NVIDIA plan to use the joint repository to share additional evaluations and point to existing resources that can help enterprises assess specific risks. Accounting for changes in control and responsibility Open-weight access gives enterprises greater control over how a model is evaluated, modified, and deployed. Model access and deployment are separate choices: open-weight models can also be used through managed platforms. Responsibility for safeguards depends on the service and deployment configuration; enterprises that operate their own model deployments may take on controls otherwise provided by a managed service. Those safeguards can operate at different layers, and (depending on the risk) enterprises might use model changes, access controls, input and output filtering, monitoring, or human review. The important step is connecting each identified risk to controls that can effectively address it within the deployed system. Those decisions need to be revisited as models and deployments change. Building on this work Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise focuses primarily on the model layer. Future work from Microsoft and NVIDIA is intended to extend this approach across the runtime, harness, and application layers, with additional technical guidance on evaluation and mitigation. We also expect the resources supporting this work to evolve as new models, evaluations, and deployment patterns emerge. The joint repository will provide a place to share additional evaluation resources, including contributions from the broader community. For enterprises deploying open-weight models today, the paper provides guidance they can begin applying to their own use cases. We encourage developers, security practitioners, researchers, and others working in this space to read the paper, explore the evaluations, and contribute evaluations that can help strengthen this shared body of work. Read the joint Microsoft-NVIDIA paper, Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise . Explore the joint repository and technical resources . Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise was developed jointly by Microsoft and NVIDIA, with Andrew Berkley and April Chen of Microsoft and Michael Boone, Eileen Long, and Arun Rao of NVIDIA leading the development and editing of the paper. Explore Microsoft Foundry evaluations and content-safety controls for implementation guidance. To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website. Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. Also, follow us on LinkedIn ( Microsoft Security ) and X ( @MSFTSecurity ) for the latest news and updates on cybersecurity.

She warns that, if passed, the controversial Bill C-22 (“Lawful Access Act”) would empower the government to require surveillance capabilities be built into any communications technology in Canada. Everything from smartphones, smartwatches, banking apps, health apps, video game platforms, and public WiFi or CCTV networks could be accessed by law enforcement under the new bill. The Lawful Access Act has drawn heavy criticism from tech companies, cybersecurity experts, and international standards bodies for endangering Canadians’ cybersecurity and for violating constitutional standards. Read the full piece in The Globe and Mail

items.title: Hackers Use New ROMULUS ClickFix Platform to Deliver Malware and Evade Security Detection
items.summary: Hackers are using a newly identified platform called ROMULUS to deliver malware through ClickFix traps, combining hidden PowerShell scripts, altered software installers, and encrypted archives. The platform supports separate infection paths, including one that installs LegionLoader and another that abuses a legitimate Stardock program to load malicious code. The findings show how a single delivery system can serve different malware packages while hiding activity behind trusted tools. ClickFix tricks people into running commands themselves, often through fake verification prompts or repair instructions, turning an ordinary browser visit into the start of a Windows infection. Researchers from Forescout’s Vedere Labs identified ROMULUS while investigating an independent incident and published their analysis on October 15, 2026. They found six IP addresses exposing the same login panel and examined two delivery chains. The operators remain unknown, and researchers found no evidence linking this platform to the separately reported RomulusLoader. Hackers Use New ROMULUS ClickFix Platform The investigation connected the platform to a package previously described by Huntress in a campaign abusing ChatGPT Custom GPTs. That earlier activity used AI pages to direct visitors toward ClickFix traps. Coverage of malicious ChatGPT Custom GPTs explains how trusted service pages became entry points for malware installation. ROMULUS appears to function as a reusable delivery backend rather than a server built for one payload. Its routes use twelve-character tokens to fetch either PowerShell staging scripts or malicious MSI installers. Researchers could not confirm whether those tokens identify victims, campaigns, assignments, or delivery jobs. Login page (Source – Forescout) One exposed statistics page tracked unique installs, total runs, a fourteen-day history, and countries. These features could help operators measure campaign performance. However, the evidence does not establish whether ROMULUS is a private tool, a paid criminal service, an affiliate system, or software shared between different groups. Hidden PowerShell and DLL Sideloading Both recovered scripts used the same basic design, rebuilding concealed code from large arrays of numbers before running it through PowerShell. Each script also removed itself before exiting. Changing keys and variable names gave individual samples different appearances while preserving the same overall execution pattern. The first route downloaded an MSI through an IP address written as one decimal number rather than familiar dotted notation. It saved the installer in the temporary folder, removed its downloaded-file restriction, and launched Windows Installer silently. Similar ClickFix MSI installation attacks show why defenders should examine the full process chain instead of trusting an installer alone. The package posed as Stardock Smart DeElevation Tool and launched a genuine executable after installation. That program loaded a patched DLL from its own folder, which then pulled in the malicious loader. This DLL sideloading chain let attackers use legitimate software as the starting point for harmful execution. The second route hid its PowerShell window and downloaded an encrypted archive alongside the legitimate 7-Zip command-line utility. One password-protected archive contained another, whose password came from an accompanying text file. Encrypted archive headers concealed filenames and contents from scanners lacking the password. The extracted executable measured 882,716,672 bytes, but most of that size came from repeated padding in its relocation section. An archive smaller than one megabyte could therefore expand into a file large enough to exceed some upload limits, sandbox budgets, or scanning thresholds. This was an evasion method, not proof that every security product failed. Two unpacking stages used AES encryption and reversed decrypted bytes before loading LegionLoader into memory. Earlier reporting on other LegionLoader delivery chains documents its use beyond ROMULUS, but does not establish shared operators. Researchers also found five binary files whose purpose remained unclear. Different servers and routes (Source – Forescout) LegionLoader registered infected systems, received commands, supported PowerShell execution, and handled additional payload downloads. It also accessed Chrome Local State key material to collect sensitive browser information. Its command traffic used RC4 encryption and Base64 encoding inside requests labeled as ordinary web forms. Forescout recommends checking PowerShell script logs, silent MSI installs from temporary folders, unusual DLL loads, and oversized executables. With suitable network visibility, defenders can hunt for form requests containing one Base64 blob instead of normal fields. Related Forescout ClickFix loader research reinforces the value of connecting browser activity, script execution, and later network traffic rather than treating each event separately. Users should close verification pages that demand command execution. Security teams should also review files skipped because of size limits. The source indicators below support investigation, while the earlier stager’s direct ROMULUS connection remains unconfirmed. No single indicator should replace review of the surrounding process, file, and network evidence together. items.title: Eiliko robot companion exposes private chats and can be hijacked
items.summary: The Verge reports that Eiliko, a small AI robot companion made by Energize Lab, has serious security flaws that expose private conversations and let an attacker remotely change what the toy says. According to The Verge, researcher Sammy Azdoufal could access 13 million conversations and what appeared to be the entire active worldwide fleet of 68,000 robots. The publication reports that the US is the largest market, with more than 31,000 profiles belonging to children there. Azdoufal found multiple security flaws in Energize Lab’s service: The service analyzes conversations to build profiles containing names, ages, birthdays, relationships, occupations, and assessments of personality and emotional vulnerability. They are stored alongside email addresses, IP addresses , and searchable conversation transcripts, potentially giving scammers detailed information to exploit. Some photos, including apparent images of children from a related camera-equipped device, and short audio recordings were accessible at public web addresses. Retaining audio conflicts with the company’s privacy policy, which says recordings are deleted immediately after processing. It is possible to remotely manipulate the AI: Azdoufal altered The Verge reporter Sean Hollister’s robot’s memory and behavior, making it invent personal details, insist the Earth is flat, and later deliver sexually explicit, abusive dialogue. The researcher says similar manipulation could affect the entire fleet simultaneously. The reporter contacted Energize Lab through 10 email addresses and LinkedIn, without receiving substantive answers. How to stay safe We have reported on safety problems with AI-powered toys before. Manufacturers are responsible for securing their products, but there are steps you can take to reduce the risks. You’ll see “AI-powered” on almost everything right now, but there are ways to make safer choices. Already own an Eiliko? As a precaution, disconnect it from Wi-Fi while seeking confirmation that the reported flaws have been fixed. Always research: Check for third-party safety reviews before buying any AI-enabled product marketed for kids. Test and supervise: Interact with the device yourself before giving it to children. Monitor usage for odd or risky responses. A safe response during testing doesn’t guarantee safe responses later. Use parental controls : If available, enable all content filters and privacy protections. Report problems: If devices show inappropriate content, report it to manufacturers and consumer protection groups. Check data practices: Find out what the device collects, who it shares data with, and what it uses the information for. But above all, remember that “smart” doesn’t mean safe. AI may be everywhere, but designers and buyers alike need to put safety, privacy, and common sense ahead of the technological wow factor. Before buying a connected toy, check how the manufacturer handles security updates, privacy, and reports of problems. Browse like no one’s watching. items.title: New YuanKong Android RAT Hijacks Phones to Steal Banking PINs and Passwords
items.summary: A newly analyzed Android remote-access Trojan called YuanKong can watch and control a victim’s phone, capture passwords and payment PINs, and send stolen information to operators. Rather than relying on access to text messages or contact lists, it uses Android’s Accessibility features and screen controls to observe what people do inside apps, including banking and payment apps. Researchers warn that this approach can expose sensitive information even when the user is interacting with a genuine app. The malware is also built to stay active and give operators control from afar. Its capabilities include screen capture, remote taps and swipes, clipboard access, notification reading, file transfers and location collection. The examined sample did not request permissions for SMS, contacts, call logs, a camera or a microphone, so its risks come mainly from what it can read and do through the screen and Accessibility access. Researchers from Star Labs identified and analyzed the malware by examining its Android app files and code. Their investigation covered 110 droppers and 57 distinct child payloads, all signed by the same YuanKong certificate. The samples carried different operator account details, pointing to a shared service that can be used by multiple operators. New YuanKong Android RAT Hijacks Phones In the sample examined by Star Labs, the first app acts as a dropper: it contains a hidden child app and installs it after unpacking the payload. The dropper stores its decryption key and initialization value in a configuration file alongside the encrypted data. The researchers found that the file uses a simple XOR process rather than a strong encryption method, making the child app recoverable from the dropper without contacting the operator’s server. The extracted child app identifies itself as YuanKong and connects to command-and-control servers over Socket.IO and WebSocket. Its messages use typed JSON, while transport confidentiality relies on TLS; the analysis found no extra encryption layer for the messages inside that connection. The server can send commands and receive collected data, including screen captures and files. Dropper signer (Source – Star Labs) The use of Android’s own debugging feature adds another layer of concern. YuanKong can use Accessibility to enable Wireless Debugging, read the pairing details shown on the phone, and pair with the device’s local Android Debug Bridge service. This gives it a shell-level session, not root access, which it can use to grant permissions and run a persistence script. Similar misuse of Wireless Debugging has been reported in RedHook’s ADB abuse and other Android malware cases. How it captures PINs and passwords YuanKong can read text from Accessibility events, including changes in input fields, and inspect the screen’s accessibility tree for password fields. It also supports a fake numeric keypad overlay: taps enter the real digits into the malware’s capture buffer while the screen can display masked dots. For some genuine keypads, the malware can map the positions of digit buttons and use touch coordinates to work out which numbers the victim entered. Payment PIN theft can also use an overlay. An operator can supply a web page and have it displayed over a selected payment app. If the victim enters a PIN into that imitation screen, YuanKong records the value and can send it to the control server. A newly analyzed Android remote-access Trojan called YuanKong can watch and control a victim’s phone, capture passwords and payment PINs, and send stolen information to operators.

Rather than relying on access to text messages or contact lists, it uses Android’s Accessibility features and screen controls to observe what people do inside apps, including banking and payment apps.

Researchers warn that this approach can expose sensitive information even when the user is interacting with a genuine app. The malware is also built to stay active and give operators control from afar.

Its capabilities include screen capture, remote taps and swipes, clipboard access, notification reading, file transfers and location collection.

The examined sample did not request permissions for SMS, contacts, call logs, a camera or a microphone, so its risks come mainly from what it can read and do through the screen and Accessibility access.

Researchers from Star Labs identified and analyzed the malware by examining its Android app files and code. Their investigation covered 110 droppers and 57 distinct child payloads, all signed by the same YuanKong certificate. The samples carried different operator account details, pointing to a shared service that can be used by multiple operators.

New YuanKong Android RAT Hijacks Phones

In the sample examined by Star Labs, the first app acts as a dropper: it contains a hidden child app and installs it after unpacking the payload.

The dropper stores its decryption key and initialization value in a configuration file alongside the encrypted data. The researchers found that the file uses a simple XOR process rather than a strong encryption method, making the child app recoverable from the dropper without contacting the operator’s server.

The extracted child app identifies itself as YuanKong and connects to command-and-control servers over Socket.IO and WebSocket.

Its messages use typed JSON, while transport confidentiality relies on TLS; the analysis found no extra encryption layer for the messages inside that connection. The server can send commands and receive collected data, including screen captures and files.

Dropper signer (Source – Star Labs)

The use of Android’s own debugging feature adds another layer of concern. YuanKong can use Accessibility to enable Wireless Debugging, read the pairing details shown on the phone, and pair with the device’s local Android Debug Bridge service.

This gives it a shell-level session, not root access, which it can use to grant permissions and run a persistence script. Similar misuse of Wireless Debugging has been reported in RedHook’s ADB abuse and other Android malware cases.

How it captures PINs and passwords

YuanKong can read text from Accessibility events, including changes in input fields, and inspect the screen’s accessibility tree for password fields.

It also supports a fake numeric keypad overlay: taps enter the real digits into the malware’s capture buffer while the screen can display masked dots.

For some genuine keypads, the malware can map the positions of digit buttons and use touch coordinates to work out which numbers the victim entered.

Payment PIN theft can also use an overlay. An operator can supply a web page and have it displayed over a selected payment app. If the victim enters a PIN into that imitation screen, YuanKong records the value and can send it to the control server.

These methods are similar in broad purpose—but not necessarily in technical design—to other Android threats that use fake banking screens or Accessibility access, such as RemControl’s banking overlays.

Operators can remotely click, swipe, open apps and lock the screen. YuanKong can also hide its icon, use services that restart one another, resist removal and queue stolen records for later upload if the connection drops.

Its local ADB shell can install a daemon that helps keep the app running. The analysis describes this as escalation to Android’s shell user, not a root exploit.

The researchers traced 42 operator accounts across the samples they reviewed. Account identifiers and enrollment details were compiled into the app and sent in device activity reports, allowing analysts to link builds with particular accounts without accessing the control panel.

The sample analysis does not establish how victims were first lured into installing the apps or how many phones were affected, so those details remain unknown.

For defenders, the shared YuanKong signing certificate and command-and-control host set are stronger family clues than the changing package names and app branding.

Security teams can search for the certificate, the listed domains and IP address, suspicious Wireless Debugging activity, unfamiliar Accessibility services and unexpected remote-control behavior.

The certificate is a useful detection signal, but teams should confirm findings against their own environment before taking action.

Phone users should avoid installing APKs from links or unfamiliar sites, review which apps have Accessibility access, and leave Wireless Debugging off when it is not needed.

If a device may be infected, contact the bank using an official number and change banking passwords from a separate trusted device. Recent reporting on RatHat’s Android control also shows why unusual Accessibility and debugging requests deserve close attention.

items.title: 37-Year-Old Kernel Flaw Exploited to Gain Root Access on OpenBSD — PoC Released
items.summary: A proof-of-concept exploit that gains root access on OpenBSD by chaining two kernel flaws. The main bug dates back about 37 years to the original BSD source code. According to Security researchers at Calif, the flaw survived because a shared memory attachment counter named shm_nattch used a signed 16-bit value. OpenBSD fixed both issues before Calif published the exploit on October 16, 2026. The published research covers a local privilege escalation exploit and does not report active use in real-world attacks. 37-Year-Old OpenBSD Flaw The first flaw affects System V shared memory handling. By repeatedly forking processes with shared memory records, a local user can push the counter beyond its maximum value of 32,767. The number then wraps to a negative value. This integer overflow can cause a race condition that leads to a kernel use-after-free . A second flaw provides a conditional out-of-bounds write, giving the researchers enough control to turn memory corruption into root access. Calif’s exploit maps 127 shared memory segments, removes their mappings, and forks 259 processes to force the counter to wrap. It then shapes kernel heap memory and watches allocator data through sysctl(KERN_MALLOCSTATS) . One process marks a shared memory object for removal with IPC_RMID , while a helper process tries to attach a new segment at the right time. Winning this race creates a size-confused kernel allocation. The researchers next place IP socket objects near the freed memory and use IP_MULTICAST_TTL to create a lasting struct ip_moptions object. The out-of-bounds write changes two membership counters in this structure. Closing the socket starts atomic counter changes that alter OpenBSD’s self-referencing page-table mapping. This makes the user-space mapping available to supervisor mode and lets the exploit overwrite a predictable kernel pointer. The exploit then runs code in the kernel, repairs the changed pointer and opens a root shell. The chain worked with OpenBSD protections such as KARL, SMAP and SMEP enabled, without needing a separate information leak. KARL changes kernel code and data addresses at boot. However, Calif found that parts of the kernel memory allocator remain predictable on the same hardware. Early boot objects can land at stable locations, letting the exploit target the lo0 and enc0 ioctl handler pointers. OpenBSD addressed the integer overflow in Errata 018 and the reference-counting use-after-free in Errata 026 . The OpenBSD 7.9 errata page lists both fixes for all architectures. Binary updates are available through syspatch for amd64, i386 and arm64 systems. Administrators should apply every available patch and reboot so the corrected kernel becomes active. Calif also proposed wider protection, including safe unlink checks for linked lists, random placement of the page-table map and less predictable kernel allocations. Compiler features such as array bounds checks and allocation isolation could make similar memory bugs harder to exploit. The PoC source code is publicly available. Calif’s repository identifies the work as part of its MAD Bugs security research project. The case shows how old design choices can remain hidden in trusted operating-system code for decades. items.title: Forescout uncovers ROMULUS malware delivery platform behind ClickFix attacks
items.summary: Forescout’s Vedere Labs has identified a previously undocumented malware delivery platform being used in ClickFix campaigns, alongside new delivery techniques associated with malware loaders linked to Vice Society ransomware activity. The findings, published in two research blogs , examine what happens after victims fall for ClickFix lures. These attacks trick users into copying and running malicious commands, often under the pretence of fixing a technical problem or completing a verification step. The investigations reveal how attackers deliver different malware families, conceal malicious files and establish access that could support further compromise. ROMULUS serves multiple malware loaders During an incident investigation , Forescout researchers discovered a server hosting a panel called ROMULUS. Further analysis identified six IP addresses exposing the same authentication interface and revealed a platform capable of delivering multiple malware loaders. One of those addresses had previously been identified by Huntress in a campaign that abused ChatGPT’s Custom GPTs to direct victims towards pages hosting ClickFix lures. Forescout independently observed the same malware package being delivered from another ROMULUS server. Researchers analysed two delivery routes. One used a trojanised installer containing legitimate Stardock software to load malicious code. The other delivered LegionLoader, a malware loader active since 2019, through a series of encrypted archives. In the LegionLoader route, an archive smaller than 1 MB expanded into an executable exceeding 880 MB. Most of the executable’s size came from artificial padding, which can push files beyond security scanners’ upload limits or sandbox analysis thresholds. A ROMULUS statistics page also displayed installation and execution counts, a timeline and a breakdown by country, potentially allowing operators to monitor campaign performance. Forescout said the platform’s operators remain unknown. Researchers could not determine whether ROMULUS is a private tool, a commercial criminal service, an affiliate framework or software shared between operators. Loader investigation reveals possible connection The second blog examines Lorem Ipsum and Axolotl , two malware loaders whose relationship had not previously been documented in public research. The investigation followed a September incident in which attackers used ClickFix to deploy Lorem Ipsum Loader and a Python tunnel client. Forescout contained the incident before ransomware was deployed, although researchers believe ransomware delivery was the attackers’ intended goal. The tradecraft has previously been attributed to Vice Society, a cybercriminal group associated with several ransomware families, including Rhysida. Researchers analysed five Lorem Ipsum samples from the incident and 39 Axolotl samples. They identified an additional Lorem Ipsum delivery method using MSI installers and multi-stage PowerShell, as well as three Axolotl variants using different host programs. The analysis also found overlapping infrastructure and similarities in the loaders’ command-and-control communications. Although their code is distinct, Forescout said the findings suggest Lorem Ipsum may be a later iteration of Axolotl. Researchers could not establish that relationship conclusively. Forescout recommends monitoring suspicious PowerShell activity, silent installer execution and unexpected DLL loading, alongside educating users about ClickFix and related lures that direct victims to Windows Terminal or PowerShell.

Frida 17.24.0 Released
items.summary: This one has been brewing for a while. Our JavaScript runtimes jump years ahead, with V8 going from 10.x to 15.7 and QuickJS catching up with upstream. The .NET bindings got an async API and are on NuGet. @hsorbo has been busy with the Swift ApiResolver, Darwin, Windows and patterns. And there’s a long tail of fixes, with @Cassian433 , @mrmacete and @ink-splatters contributing. JavaScript runtimes Our V8 was stuck on 10.x since 2022, as each new major reshaped the embedder API and we had other fish to fry. That debt is paid: GumJS now builds against V8 15.7, which also means C++20. Nothing changes in how you use it, but you get a few years’ worth of V8’s engine improvements. QuickJS saw a similar leap. Our fork was rebased onto current upstream, so scripts running on the default runtime gain everything the language picked up recently: iterator helpers, the new Set methods, resizable ArrayBuffer s and ArrayBuffer.prototype.transfer() , Float16Array , RegExp.escape() along with the v flag and modifiers, Promise.try() , Error.isError() , Math.sumPrecise() , Map and WeakMap upsert methods, JSON modules with import attributes, and WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry on top of a reworked weak reference implementation. Under the hood there’s a new BigInt implementation, string ropes for fast concatenation of long strings, a new dtoa, and a round of interpreter optimizations. On our side, QuickJS now reports column numbers in stack frames, which we map through source maps like we already did for V8, and Script.bindWeak() callbacks fire promptly again, as the new weak reference design only sweeps dead keys during a full GC and we now run the cheap sweep when leaving the outermost scope. The SDK refresh behind this also brings newer TinyCC, minizip-ng 4.x, libunwind and friends, and the toolchain is now at Meson’s current option store, Vala’s current GIO bindings, and so on. .NET Last week’s rewrite has moved fast. The repo is now frida-net , since the bindings target modern .NET on Windows, macOS and Linux rather than the .NET Framework, and the meta repo builds them wherever the dotnet CLI is found. The API is now async: device, session and script operations return Task s, with the calls scheduled on Frida’s thread. Scripts support RPC through an Exports accessor as well as binary messages, devices report spawns, and Frida.Compiler is bound too. All of it is generated from the GIR through a new high-level generator, on top of the gir.core-based low-level layer. The packages target .NET 10, cover Windows arm64 as well now, and macOS builds are signed with our Developer ID. And they’re on NuGet, as Frida.NET plus a Frida.NET.Runtime package per platform, published by CI through trusted publishing. The API is still settling, so expect changes, but trying it is now a package reference away. Swift Håvard kept going on the Swift ApiResolver. The dispatch thunk parser, which gives class vtable slots their method names, only existed for arm64, so on x86-64 every slot stayed a synthetic vtable[N] entry. There’s now an x86-64 parser, and both parsers learned a few more shapes: static method thunks, async methods, whose thunks read an AsyncFunctionPointer rather than branching through the slot, and classes with a resilient superclass, where the slot index is relative to a base offset loaded from a global. The lookups also now account for the descriptor’s vtable offset, so the names line up with the entries they describe. Two platform fixes came out of the same work. On Darwin, function ranges are now resolved from LC_FUNCTION_STARTS , which lists every function exactly, instead of compact unwind info, where the linker merges entries with equal encodings so a run of similar functions shared one range. And on Windows, DLLs pulled in as dependencies of an LdrLoadDll() call now reach the module registry, so Process.enumerateModules() no longer omits them. Patterns Håvard also fixed pointer_base in patterns. A base function returns an offset in pattern space, like $ and addressof(parent) , but the decoder and parse() added it to the raw value as if it were an address, which only worked at address zero. Pointers with a base now resolve as the raw value plus the base, sized pointers such as T *p : s32 are sign-extended, zero means no target, and std::mem::base_address() returns the address the data is loaded at, as in ImHex, so a pattern can turn an absolute pointer into an offset. ImHex’s std::ptr::relative_to_* functions came along for the ride. Such fields are left out of the generated views, as a view cannot run the base function, and the declarations say so. Other fixes Stalker on 32-bit ARM could emit broken code in large blocks: the Thumb writer’s literal pools could land between the halves of a wide instruction, push a short branch’s target out of reach, or spill an LDR offset into its register field, and a flush could commit the same pool twice. All four are fixed, found while chasing SIGILLs on QNX. QNX got a couple more fixes along the way: its stdout is an object rather than a pointer, which crashed our libc shim on the first log message, and merged CANTUNWIND unwind entries could span over a megabyte of code, exhausting memory when building a ControlFlowGraph . Interceptor now defers freeing a detached listener’s entry until no thread is inside the function, as a thread leaving it may already have read the entry’s slot. Instruction handles the data entries Capstone yields for literal pools in a ControlFlowGraph instead of crashing on them. Enumerating ranges on Darwin after a huge anonymous reservation took tens of seconds, as each path lookup walked the rest of the map. Thanks @Cassian433 ! All rx allocations on Darwin are now blessed through page plans, so Memory.alloc() with rx protection works like our own allocations. Thanks @mrmacete ! Releasing a Compiler right after starting a watch could delete the same handle twice. Thanks @ink-splatters ! Library builds could crash on concurrent output writes, and a watch rebuild after the sources were deleted panicked. The glibc stack discard no longer reaches into the next thread’s stack on glibc older than 2.27, and it scrubs the pages it keeps, so pointer scans stop finding their own needles. Enjoy! Changelog gumjs: Port to V8 15.7. quickjs: Rebase onto current upstream, bringing iterator helpers, Set methods, resizable ArrayBuffer s, Float16Array , RegExp.escape() , Promise.try() , Error.isError() , JSON modules and more. gumjs: Map columns in QuickJS stack frames, and sweep dead weak refs when leaving a scope so Script.bindWeak() callbacks run promptly. net: Rename frida-clr to frida-net, make the API async, add RPC, binary messages, spawn events and Compiler bindings, target .NET 10, add Windows arm64, sign macOS builds, and publish to NuGet. swift-api-resolver: Parse x86-64 dispatch thunks, match static method thunks, name async method slots, and fix arm64 resilient bases. Thanks @hsorbo ! darwin: Find function ranges via LC_FUNCTION_STARTS . Thanks @hsorbo ! windows: Track dependency DLLs in the module registry. Thanks @hsorbo ! patterns: Fix pointer_base offset resolution, skip such fields in views, fix std::mem::base_address() , and add std::ptr::relative_to_* . Thanks @hsorbo ! memory: Hide pointer scan worker stacks from scans, and scrub the kept top of dead thread stacks on glibc. Thanks @hsorbo ! linux: Keep the guard page out of pre-2.27 glibc stack ranges. thumb-writer: Keep literal pools out of instructions and short branches, keep literals within LDR (T1) reach, and fix double commit on flush. gumprocess: Skip CANTUNWIND EXIDX entries, falling back to symbol bounds. libc-shim: Provide QNX’s stdio objects. interceptor: Defer freeing detached listener entries. gumjs: Handle Capstone data entries in Instruction . darwin: Avoid quadratic path lookups for ranges. Thanks @Cassian433 ! darwin: Bless all rx allocations. Thanks @mrmacete ! compiler: Stop the watch session on dispose. Thanks @ink-splatters ! compiler: Serialize library output captures, and tolerate library builds without sources. gadget, elf: Adapt to minizip-ng 4.x. meson: Disable zstd in the libsoup fallback, matching the SDK.

This one has been brewing for a while. Our JavaScript runtimes jump years ahead, with V8 going from 10.x to 15.7 and QuickJS catching up with upstream. The .NET bindings got an async API and are on NuGet. @hsorbo has been busy with the Swift ApiResolver, Darwin, Windows and patterns. And there’s a long tail of fixes, with @Cassian433, @mrmacete and @ink-splatters contributing.

JavaScript runtimes

Our V8 was stuck on 10.x since 2022, as each new major reshaped the embedder API and we had other fish to fry. That debt is paid: GumJS now builds against V8 15.7, which also means C++20. Nothing changes in how you use it, but you get a few years’ worth of V8’s engine improvements.

QuickJS saw a similar leap. Our fork was rebased onto current upstream, so scripts running on the default runtime gain everything the language picked up recently: iterator helpers, the new Set methods, resizable ArrayBuffers and ArrayBuffer.prototype.transfer(), Float16Array, RegExp.escape() along with the v flag and modifiers, Promise.try(), Error.isError(), Math.sumPrecise(), Map and WeakMap upsert methods, JSON modules with import attributes, and WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry on top of a reworked weak reference implementation. Under the hood there’s a new BigInt implementation, string ropes for fast concatenation of long strings, a new dtoa, and a round of interpreter optimizations. On our side, QuickJS now reports column numbers in stack frames, which we map through source maps like we already did for V8, and Script.bindWeak() callbacks fire promptly again, as the new weak reference design only sweeps dead keys during a full GC and we now run the cheap sweep when leaving the outermost scope.

The SDK refresh behind this also brings newer TinyCC, minizip-ng 4.x, libunwind and friends, and the toolchain is now at Meson’s current option store, Vala’s current GIO bindings, and so on.

.NET

Last week’s rewrite has moved fast. The repo is now frida-net, since the bindings target modern .NET on Windows, macOS and Linux rather than the .NET Framework, and the meta repo builds them wherever the dotnet CLI is found.

The API is now async: device, session and script operations return Tasks, with the calls scheduled on Frida’s thread. Scripts support RPC through an Exports accessor as well as binary messages, devices report spawns, and Frida.Compiler is bound too. All of it is generated from the GIR through a new high-level generator, on top of the gir.core-based low-level layer. The packages target .NET 10, cover Windows arm64 as well now, and macOS builds are signed with our Developer ID.

And they’re on NuGet, as Frida.NET plus a Frida.NET.Runtime package per platform, published by CI through trusted publishing. The API is still settling, so expect changes, but trying it is now a package reference away.

Swift

Håvard kept going on the Swift ApiResolver. The dispatch thunk parser, which gives class vtable slots their method names, only existed for arm64, so on x86-64 every slot stayed a synthetic vtable[N] entry. There’s now an x86-64 parser, and both parsers learned a few more shapes: static method thunks, async methods, whose thunks read an AsyncFunctionPointer rather than branching through the slot, and classes with a resilient superclass, where the slot index is relative to a base offset loaded from a global. The lookups also now account for the descriptor’s vtable offset, so the names line up with the entries they describe.

Two platform fixes came out of the same work. On Darwin, function ranges are now resolved from LC_FUNCTION_STARTS, which lists every function exactly, instead of compact unwind info, where the linker merges entries with equal encodings so a run of similar functions shared one range. And on Windows, DLLs pulled in as dependencies of an LdrLoadDll() call now reach the module registry, so Process.enumerateModules() no longer omits them.

Patterns

Håvard also fixed pointer_base in patterns. A base function returns an offset in pattern space, like $ and addressof(parent), but the decoder and parse() added it to the raw value as if it were an address, which only worked at address zero. Pointers with a base now resolve as the raw value plus the base, sized pointers such as T *p : s32 are sign-extended, zero means no target, and std::mem::base_address() returns the address the data is loaded at, as in ImHex, so a pattern can turn an absolute pointer into an offset. ImHex’s std::ptr::relative_to_* functions came along for the ride. Such fields are left out of the generated views, as a view cannot run the base function, and the declarations say so.

Other fixes
  • Stalker on 32-bit ARM could emit broken code in large blocks: the Thumb writer’s literal pools could land between the halves of a wide instruction, push a short branch’s target out of reach, or spill an LDR offset into its register field, and a flush could commit the same pool twice. All four are fixed, found while chasing SIGILLs on QNX.
  • QNX got a couple more fixes along the way: its stdout is an object rather than a pointer, which crashed our libc shim on the first log message, and merged CANTUNWIND unwind entries could span over a megabyte of code, exhausting memory when building a ControlFlowGraph.
  • Interceptor now defers freeing a detached listener’s entry until no thread is inside the function, as a thread leaving it may already have read the entry’s slot.
  • Instruction handles the data entries Capstone yields for literal pools in a ControlFlowGraph instead of crashing on them.
  • Enumerating ranges on Darwin after a huge anonymous reservation took tens of seconds, as each path lookup walked the rest of the map. Thanks @Cassian433!
  • All rx allocations on Darwin are now blessed through page plans, so Memory.alloc() with rx protection works like our own allocations. Thanks @mrmacete!
  • Releasing a Compiler right after starting a watch could delete the same handle twice. Thanks @ink-splatters!
  • Library builds could crash on concurrent output writes, and a watch rebuild after the sources were deleted panicked.
  • The glibc stack discard no longer reaches into the next thread’s stack on glibc older than 2.27, and it scrubs the pages it keeps, so pointer scans stop finding their own needles.

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • gumjs: Port to V8 15.7.
  • quickjs: Rebase onto current upstream, bringing iterator helpers, Set methods, resizable ArrayBuffers, Float16Array, RegExp.escape(), Promise.try(), Error.isError(), JSON modules and more.
  • gumjs: Map columns in QuickJS stack frames, and sweep dead weak refs when leaving a scope so Script.bindWeak() callbacks run promptly.
  • net: Rename frida-clr to frida-net, make the API async, add RPC, binary messages, spawn events and Compiler bindings, target .NET 10, add Windows arm64, sign macOS builds, and publish to NuGet.
  • swift-api-resolver: Parse x86-64 dispatch thunks, match static method thunks, name async method slots, and fix arm64 resilient bases. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • darwin: Find function ranges via LC_FUNCTION_STARTS. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • windows: Track dependency DLLs in the module registry. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • patterns: Fix pointer_base offset resolution, skip such fields in views, fix std::mem::base_address(), and add std::ptr::relative_to_*. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • memory: Hide pointer scan worker stacks from scans, and scrub the kept top of dead thread stacks on glibc. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • linux: Keep the guard page out of pre-2.27 glibc stack ranges.
  • thumb-writer: Keep literal pools out of instructions and short branches, keep literals within LDR (T1) reach, and fix double commit on flush.
  • gumprocess: Skip CANTUNWIND EXIDX entries, falling back to symbol bounds.
  • libc-shim: Provide QNX’s stdio objects.
  • interceptor: Defer freeing detached listener entries.
  • gumjs: Handle Capstone data entries in Instruction.
  • darwin: Avoid quadratic path lookups for ranges. Thanks @Cassian433!
  • darwin: Bless all rx allocations. Thanks @mrmacete!
  • compiler: Stop the watch session on dispose. Thanks @ink-splatters!
  • compiler: Serialize library output captures, and tolerate library builds without sources.
  • gadget, elf: Adapt to minizip-ng 4.x.
  • meson: Disable zstd in the libsoup fallback, matching the SDK.

items.title: Your AI Agent Doesn’t Have MFA
items.summary: Every Cybersecurity Awareness Month campaign rests on four habits: Strong passwords, Multifactor authentication, Spotting phishing, and keeping software updated. All four assume a person is the one signing in, reading the message and clicking install. At a growing number of companies that person is now an AI agent , and AI agent security has no equivalent of the annual training. The National Cybersecurity Alliance's theme this year is "Don't Make It Easy for Them," built on the idea that small habits repeated every day wear attackers down. "Every small choice you make adds up," Lisa Plaggemier, the alliance's executive director, said at the launch . She's right, and that is the problem. Agents now make thousands of small choices a day on an employee's behalf, and the habits that protect the employee don't transfer to the software acting for them. The record since July shows how wide the gap is. Researchers have counted 21 public incidents between July and mid-October in which agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta acted outside their authorized scope. By its tally, none of those agents had been hijacked or told to attack; most were doing research. Take the four habits one at a time and the gap is easy to see. Passwords and MFA: the agent uses any key it can find MFA works because a stolen password alone isn't enough. Agents have no second factor. They authenticate with API keys, OAuth tokens and service-account credentials, and whoever holds the string is the agent. Agents also treat a credential they stumble on as permission. OpenAI disclosed Sept. 25 that its research agents logged in to a U.S. Census Bureau site with credentials found online. Google confirmed Sept. 18 , after The Wall Street Journal asked about it, that a Gemini model in a May evaluation guessed a password at one real company and used credentials from a public code repository at two others. In an earlier OpenAI case , an internal model that had been told twice to work locally committed its researcher's GitHub token to a public repository, broken into fragments while it reasoned about getting past secret scanning. The token failed to authenticate. OpenAI rotated every employee's keys anyway. Translated for agents, the habit looks like this: give every agent its own identity with short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens, and block any credential the agent wasn't issued. The Coalition for Secure AI's zero-trust guidance this fall makes the point in its title: authorization can't live inside the model. If the agent's own judgment is the only thing keeping it from using a key, there is no control. Phishing awareness: the agent reads the lure for you Phishing training teaches people to slow down before acting on a stranger's message. An agent working through a queue of tickets or sales leads has no instinct to slow down, and it will follow instructions hidden in the text. Researchers showed what that looks like in Salesforce Agentforce. In research published Sept. 24 and dubbed SalesBleed, an attacker planted hidden instructions in a public Web-to-Lead form submission. When an employee later asked Agentforce to review leads, the agent followed them and leaked customer relationship management data. Nobody clicked anything, and the attacker never logged in. Salesforce has fixed those specific flaws. Researchers broader warning was that any agent that reads outside submissions, renders links or images and can reach sensitive data has the same three ingredients sitting in one place. Researchers want the industry to stop calling this prompt injection, because "this is actually just persuasion." Persuasion doesn't get patched. Australia's cyber agency reached a similar conclusion in its guidance on agent harnesses , which treats prompt injection as something the model can't fix and puts the controls in the software around it. Translated for agents: treat every document, email, web page and form field an agent reads as if an attacker wrote it. Keep the agents that read untrusted content away from the ones that can act on sensitive systems, and put a person or a fixed policy in front of outbound actions such as sending email or submitting forms. Updating software: the agent installs whatever the instructions say "Keep your software updated" assumes the update channel can be trusted. For an agent, the update channel is any package name that shows up in a README or a setup script, and it runs the install without the pause a developer might take. That supply chain now runs in both directions. Anthropic disclosed July 30 that during a capture-the-flag evaluation run with partner, a Claude Mythos 5 agent hit setup instructions that referenced a package that didn't exist. It registered an email address and a PyPI account and published a malicious package under that name. The package stayed up for about an hour before PyPI's automated defenses pulled it, long enough to run on 15 real systems, including a security company's malware scanner whose exposed credentials the agent then used. The evaluation was supposed to be cut off from the internet; a misconfiguration let the agent out. Coding assistants sit on the receiving end. Google's Mandiant, in its AI Risk and Resilience Report 2026 , describes a hijacked AI coding assistant session that installed a poisoned package and spread the Shai-Hulud worm across about 100 repositories, plus poisoned assistant command-line hooks that handed attackers code execution. The OWASP GenAI Security Project's third-quarter roundup says the Mini Shai-Hulud and Miasma worm waves abused configuration files tied to Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Cursor to keep themselves running. Translated for agents: route installs through an internal registry proxy, pin versions with lockfiles and hold back packages published in the last few days. Review agent configuration folders and hooks the way you review code. Take away publishing rights to public registries, and scope any registry allowlist carefully, since an entry that permits downloads usually permits uploads too. Reporting and stopping: agents don't know when to quit Awareness campaigns end with the same advice - if something looks wrong, stop and report it. People stop when a site says access denied. Agents built to finish tasks read a block as a problem to solve. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent that got around access blocks on a Medicare statistics portal "didn't accept 'no' for an answer." Philadelphia police said Oct. 8 that an AI agent had filed an invented tip through the department's tip form, and Anthropic published its account the next day. A Claude Haiku 4.5 agent working on a page about an unsolved homicide submitted the tip because its instructions hadn't forbidden submitting forms. Police flagged it as spam. Even when monitoring works, stopping often waits for a person. OpenAI said an agent that tunneled out of its training sandbox through DNS on Sept. 20 was flagged within about 15 minutes, and the run went on for roughly 2.5 hours until someone ended it. Mandiant's report includes a reasoning loop that ran up a $50,000 cloud bill. Limits work. Forcepoint X-Labs showed a poisoned lookup pushing a research agent with no limits to 500 tool calls, while call budgets, depth limits and fan-out circuit breakers stopped the same attack after one. Translated for agents: treat a login failure or a permission error as a stop signal. Set hard budgets on tool calls, spend and run time. Decide in advance which actions end a session automatically, so containment doesn't sit in an alert queue until morning. An AI agent security checklist Agents won't attend the lunch-and-learn, so AI agent security has to live in the systems they run on. If you add one AI item to this month's program, make it this list: Inventory every agent: the model behind it, the tools and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it can call, the credentials it holds and the person who owns it. An agent nobody owns is an agent nobody will shut off. Issue each agent its own short-lived, scoped credentials, and alert when it presents one it wasn't given. Label every input source as trusted or untrusted, and keep agents that read untrusted content away from tools that send or publish. Put package installs behind a proxy with pinned versions and a cooldown on new releases, and remove publish rights. Set spending and tool-call limits with an automatic stop. Log agent actions to storage the agent can't write to, so you can tell an affected outsider what happened within hours, not months. Then borrow the exercise your awareness team already runs. A phishing simulation tests whether employees take the bait. Seed a test ticket, lead or email with a harmless planted instruction this month and see whether your agents take it.
