items.title: Hackers Use AI-Generated Scripts to Hijack Linux Sudo Commands and Steal Passwords
items.summary: A campaign against government organizations and state-linked infrastructure used AI-assisted scripts to steal credentials, maintain access to Linux servers and seek sensitive data, according to new research. The attackers altered users’ shell startup files to intercept the sudo command, then copied entered passwords to a file while passing them to the real command. This let a user’s request appear to work normally as the password was stolen. Unit 42’s investigation says the activity also involved web shells, custom malware, mailbox searches and attempts to erase evidence. The operation shows how familiar Linux tools can be turned against their users. Rather than exploiting a flaw in sudo itself, the attackers planted a malicious alias in .bashrc , a file that runs commands when a user starts a Bash shell. The distinction matters: applying a software patch alone would not remove this kind of tampering. Administrators may find this earlier Linux sudo vulnerability useful context, but Unit 42 described credential interception through a changed shell configuration, not that vulnerability. Researchers from Unit 42 identified the activity and track the group of related operations as CL-UNK-1211. They observed activity from October 2025 to April 2026 targeting government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure. Unit 42 uses “UNK” for clusters whose links to either state-backed activity or cybercrime have not been determined, so the findings do not identify a known government or criminal group as responsible. Several scripts contained conversational comments and step-by-step reasoning notes that researchers said were consistent with AI-generated code or an automated AI agent. The evidence points to AI helping create or adapt parts of the toolkit; it does not establish that AI independently planned or carried out the campaign. Snippets of code containing comments, indicating the use of AI (Source – Unit42) Unit 42 also noted Base64-encoded commands and scripts that moved between PHP, JavaScript, Bash and Python. These clues may help defenders spot suspicious code, but they are not proof of AI use on their own. Hackers Use AI-Generated Scripts The attackers replaced a user’s .bashrc with a modified copy containing an alias for sudo . When the user ran the command, the alias displayed a prompt resembling the normal password request, captured the password and wrote it to an attacker-controlled log file. It then passed the password to the legitimate sudo command, making the interception less obvious. The attackers named the file Solarwinds.StatusLog.txt , apparently to make it look like a routine system artifact. Unit 42 said it found no evidence that SolarWinds systems or infrastructure were compromised. The credential theft did not stop at the shell. Attackers also inserted code into a PHP login page to collect administrator usernames and passwords, and searched configuration files and command histories for email, SMTP and database credentials. The campaign’s use of web shells and hidden access has parallels with other Linux credential-stealing malware , though that article describes a separate threat and should not be confused with CL-UNK-1211. Malware, persistence and data theft Unit 42 found a custom Go-based remote access Trojan it named SysGoRAT. The malware can run on Linux and Windows, communicate with a command-and-control server over WebSocket and support remote commands, shell access, file handling and persistence. Attackers used names such as sys-control-client , pip2.7 and ea_install to disguise the binary. Its default C2 address was 104.194.158[.]65:443 , though the report says operators could change it at launch. The attackers also deployed web shells and changed PHP configuration so a malicious file would load before other PHP scripts. They searched government mailboxes for messages related to social media accounts, attempted to package mailbox contents and sought database data. Unit 42 reported that one mailbox-archiving script contained a syntax error and would fail as written. The finding is a reminder that observed malicious code does not always work as intended. To hide their presence, operators tried to stop endpoint security processes, delete logs and shell history, remove temporary scripts after use and change file timestamps. Interactive web shell activity, as shown in Cortex XDR (Source – Unit42) They also planted red-team-like markers, including RedTeamOps2025 and pentest123 , to make activity appear authorized. Unit 42 said endpoint protections detected and stopped attempts to terminate Cortex XDR processes; that result concerns the observed systems and does not mean every attempted activity was blocked. The campaign fits a broader pattern of attackers using AI to speed up script development, as seen in other AI-generated malware research . For defenders, the practical response is to review unexpected changes to .bashrc , PHP settings and login pages; check for unfamiliar aliases or credential log files; monitor unusual outbound connections and shell activity; and preserve logs and system evidence during an investigation. The indicators below are from Unit 42’s report and should be checked against local telemetry before being treated as evidence of compromise. This let a user’s request appear to work normally as the password was stolen. Unit 42’s investigation says the activity also involved web shells, custom malware, mailbox searches and attempts to erase evidence.

The operation shows how familiar Linux tools can be turned against their users. Rather than exploiting a flaw in sudo itself, the attackers planted a malicious alias in .bashrc, a file that runs commands when a user starts a Bash shell.

The distinction matters: applying a software patch alone would not remove this kind of tampering. Administrators may find this earlier Linux sudo vulnerability useful context, but Unit 42 described credential interception through a changed shell configuration, not that vulnerability.

Researchers from Unit 42 identified the activity and track the group of related operations as CL-UNK-1211. They observed activity from October 2025 to April 2026 targeting government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure.

Unit 42 uses “UNK” for clusters whose links to either state-backed activity or cybercrime have not been determined, so the findings do not identify a known government or criminal group as responsible.

Several scripts contained conversational comments and step-by-step reasoning notes that researchers said were consistent with AI-generated code or an automated AI agent.

The evidence points to AI helping create or adapt parts of the toolkit; it does not establish that AI independently planned or carried out the campaign.

Snippets of code containing comments, indicating the use of AI (Source – Unit42)

Unit 42 also noted Base64-encoded commands and scripts that moved between PHP, JavaScript, Bash and Python. These clues may help defenders spot suspicious code, but they are not proof of AI use on their own.

Hackers Use AI-Generated Scripts

The attackers replaced a user’s .bashrc with a modified copy containing an alias for sudo. When the user ran the command, the alias displayed a prompt resembling the normal password request, captured the password and wrote it to an attacker-controlled log file.

It then passed the password to the legitimate sudo command, making the interception less obvious. The attackers named the file Solarwinds.StatusLog.txt, apparently to make it look like a routine system artifact. Unit 42 said it found no evidence that SolarWinds systems or infrastructure were compromised.

The credential theft did not stop at the shell. Attackers also inserted code into a PHP login page to collect administrator usernames and passwords, and searched configuration files and command histories for email, SMTP and database credentials.

The campaign’s use of web shells and hidden access has parallels with other Linux credential-stealing malware, though that article describes a separate threat and should not be confused with CL-UNK-1211.

Malware, persistence and data theft

Unit 42 found a custom Go-based remote access Trojan it named SysGoRAT. The malware can run on Linux and Windows, communicate with a command-and-control server over WebSocket and support remote commands, shell access, file handling and persistence.

Attackers used names such as sys-control-client, pip2.7 and ea_install to disguise the binary. Its default C2 address was 104.194.158[.]65:443, though the report says operators could change it at launch.

The attackers also deployed web shells and changed PHP configuration so a malicious file would load before other PHP scripts. They searched government mailboxes for messages related to social media accounts, attempted to package mailbox contents and sought database data.

Unit 42 reported that one mailbox-archiving script contained a syntax error and would fail as written. The finding is a reminder that observed malicious code does not always work as intended.

To hide their presence, operators tried to stop endpoint security processes, delete logs and shell history, remove temporary scripts after use and change file timestamps.

Interactive web shell activity, as shown in Cortex XDR (Source – Unit42)

They also planted red-team-like markers, including RedTeamOps2025 and pentest123, to make activity appear authorized. Unit 42 said endpoint protections detected and stopped attempts to terminate Cortex XDR processes; that result concerns the observed systems and does not mean every attempted activity was blocked.

The campaign fits a broader pattern of attackers using AI to speed up script development, as seen in other AI-generated malware research.

For defenders, the practical response is to review unexpected changes to .bashrc, PHP settings and login pages; check for unfamiliar aliases or credential log files; monitor unusual outbound connections and shell activity; and preserve logs and system evidence during an investigation.

The indicators below are from Unit 42’s report and should be checked against local telemetry before being treated as evidence of compromise.

items.title: Continuous accountability for Verified bots
items.summary: A driver’s license tells you who someone is and that they passed a driving test, not whether they’ll drive responsibly in the future. The same is true for bots: verifying who operates it creates accountability, but trust depends on what it does next. A known bot can still ignore website preferences, overwhelm origins, or evade controls. It’s not always malicious — often it’s just a misconfiguration or a bug. As we described in a previous blog post on bot behavior, we strive to verify two questions: “Are you who you say you are?” and “Can we trust you?” To be a Cloudflare Verified Bot, you broadly need to meet three criteria: Identify yourself accurately and securely Do only what you say you will do Don’t engage in abusive behavior Bots use Web Bot Auth to sign requests that establish their identity, which BotBase then catalogues in an open format. With identification addressed, our focus shifts to the second cardinal rule of Verified bots: thou shalt do no harm . Today we introduce a system to evaluate and report when Verified bot behavior starts to deviate from this rule, ensuring that the answer to “Can we trust you?” remains “Yes.” This is where the distinction between risk and trust becomes important: Risk describes the likelihood that a particular request or point-in-time action may be harmful, and it can change from one moment to the next. Trust is built over time through repeated and consistent behavior. For example, we de-listed Perplexity’s bot from our Verified bot list in 2025 when it sought to access resources on websites that opted out of scraping and subsequently attempted to circumvent controls when those requests were blocked. Do not engage in abusive behavior This simple requirement sounds like a freebie, but there is a lot of nuance in that statement. When crawlers don’t respect site preferences , that undermines trust. When sites request a crawler to not crawl or to slow down, and the crawler ignores these requests, that undermines trust. We developed a system to measure how often a crawler respects site preferences. These observations will translate to an explainable trust band: a range showing how consistently a bot respects site preferences and which observed behaviors informed that assessment, rather than a permanent judgment about a bot or its operator. The initial signals we evaluate are: Does the bot respect instructions? Did it respond to direct feedback? We consider these to be “common sense” rules, a courtesy to the operators who provide the information bots seek. In the future, we will be sharing these scores publicly on Radar , as well as expanding the ways we measure. This score gives responsible bot operators a way to demonstrate that trust is being upheld over time. Verify, but continuously re-verify. When in Rome, do as the Romans do A robots.txt file is the primary way to communicate site owner preferences. Our system considers whether a bot’s observed traffic is consistent with those published preferences over time. Robots.txt tells all (or specific) bots to only crawl specific parts of a website. Isolated violations and other types of one-offs may not be significant. What we look for instead are repeated patterns of behavior that disregards site preferences. The expectation is simply for responsible bots to consult and honor the preferences that websites publish, in line with RFC 9309 . And just to be clear, a robots.txt sets the minimum rules for what bots and agents should not do. But there is no implication that anything not stated is allowed. For example, a robots.txt does not need to say that a bot must stop when the site can communicate that continued access is unwelcome through other signals. What you do not wish for yourself, do not impose on others Bots can remain entirely within allowed paths while still placing substantial load on the websites they visit. One of the clearest ways a website can push back is with an HTTP 429 (“Too Many Requests”) response. A 429 is a directive for the visitor to reduce its request rate, sometimes with guidance about how long to wait before trying again. Our system considers whether the bot’s traffic adapts after receiving that signal. Does it slow down, pause, or does it continue sending requests at the same pace? We then incorporate that behavior into the bot’s trust band over time: consistently slowing down or pausing increases trust, while repeatedly ignoring the signal lowers it. Building trust over time Observing these signals is only a first step toward making verified automation accountable over time. By pairing bot identity with evidence of continuing behavior, we can give site owners more confidence that the bots they choose to allow are respecting their preferences, give bot operators a way to demonstrate they deserve trust, and provide context to website owners about the automated traffic reaching them. This system, alongside Bot Preference Sync and Bot Management , forms an accountability loop for automated traffic. Bot Preference Sync helps website owners publish their preferences, and observing how bots interact with these preferences shows whether Verified bots consistently honor them over time. Bot Management lets website owners decide how that traffic is handled. Together, they help ensure that trust is earned through transparent, accountable behavior, not assumed from identity alone. We are already using this system internally to evaluate how consistently Verified bots honor website preferences. Because trust is built over time, we assess sustained patterns rather than isolated events. We are using this initial phase to build that history and refine how those observations become useful guidance. Building on that foundation, we plan to make the system available to all Cloudflare customers, who will be able to choose the trust threshold used to decide how Verified bot traffic is handled. Our goal is straightforward: to keep website preferences meaningful, and ensure trust is earned through sustained behavior. Want to learn more about how you can handle bots? Cloudflare customers can already use Bot Management to manage automated traffic and Bot Preference Sync to align their published preferences with their configured policies. To explore the ever-growing Verified bot population, see the trends on Radar . And if you are interested in helping build the future of bot identity and accountability, explore open roles at Cloudflare .

For example, we de-listed Perplexity’s bot from our Verified bot list in 2025 when it sought to access resources on websites that opted out of scraping and subsequently attempted to circumvent controls when those requests were blocked.

This simple requirement sounds like a freebie, but there is a lot of nuance in that statement. When crawlers don’t respect site preferences, that undermines trust. When sites request a crawler to not crawl or to slow down, and the crawler ignores these requests, that undermines trust.

items.title: Hackers Abuse 20,000 Cloudflare Pages Domains to Push Fake Microsoft Security Alerts
items.summary: Hackers have abused more than 20,000 Cloudflare Pages domains over six months to spread fake Microsoft security alerts and steer users toward scam call centers. The campaign uses Help Traffic Distribution System, or Help TDS, to route visitors from compromised websites, malicious ads, social media, and spam into tech support scams. The pages claim that Microsoft has disabled the computer, play loud alarms, and display a support number. A browser lock makes the device appear unusable, pushing victims to call someone posing as a Microsoft technician. The goal is remote access, not simply a payment for fake repairs. Infoblox researchers identified the malware-linked operation and assessed that Hotejka, a Russian-language affiliate program, runs Help TDS. Their October 15 research report links Hotejka to ROI777 through historical DNS records, shared infrastructure, affiliate identifiers, and access to its affiliate panel. The operation dates to at least April 2017. Hackers Abuse 20,000 Cloudflare Pages Domains Help TDS checks browser details and location before choosing where to send each visitor. Selected users see a fake update notice followed by Microsoft-branded warnings. Earlier reporting on Help TDS website redirects described how malicious PHP templates and WordPress plugins turn legitimate websites into entry points for similar scams. Infoblox tested the call center in June 2026. An operator claimed to represent Microsoft Technical Support, asked whether the computer belonged to a person or business, and helped remove the browser lock. He then instructed the researchers to download UltraViewer, a legitimate remote desktop tool that attackers can misuse for system access. The Help TDS ecosystem (Source – Infoblox) The call ended after researchers questioned why additional software was needed. This distinction matters: UltraViewer is not presented as a custom malware payload. The scam relies on convincing users to install remote access software themselves, creating access that could support data theft or further attacks. Disposable Cloudflare Pages Infrastructure Since April 2026, the group has hosted its TDS and scam pages on disposable Cloudflare Pages sites. It announces roughly 300 fresh domains daily through Telegram. Previous coverage of Cloudflare developer domain abuse shows how criminals also use these services for phishing redirects and fake verification pages. Infoblox detected another 10,000 Pages domains apparently tied to phishing or decoy activity, beyond the 20,000 associated with the core operation. Screenshots of May 2026 advertisements from Hotejka on open forums (Source – Infoblox) Some pages show harmless-looking advertisements during direct scans, helping hide their role. These figures describe attacker-created infrastructure, not 20,000 compromised Cloudflare customer accounts. The affiliate code retrieves current routing domains from Telegram, uses a fallback server, and refreshes cached results every 30 seconds. It can limit scam displays to call center working hours. GoDaddy previously documented the malicious WordPress plugin infrastructure supporting these redirects. Infoblox identified about 20 affiliates, including Balada Injector, Detour Dog, and DollyWay. Earlier research into DollyWay WordPress malware infections explains how compromised sites feed traffic into scam networks, linking website infections to the visitors who eventually encounter fake alerts. Infoblox says its detection models identify related domains about seven days before use. Exposure among its cloud customers fell from daily peaks of 4% to below 0.5% in September. These are vendor-specific exposure figures, not confirmed infection rates or measures of the entire campaign. items.title: CVE-2026-102764: Critical BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Exploited by China-Linked Hackers
items.summary: BeyondTrust has disclosed CVE-2026-102764, a critical vulnerability in Remote Support (RS) that was exploited as a zero-day by a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage actor. The flaw carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3 and can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to perform arbitrary file operations on a vulnerable appliance. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant attribute the observed exploitation to ARMORY CASTLE, formerly tracked as UNC5221 and also associated with the name WARP PANDA. The group has a history of targeting internet-facing security appliances and exploiting previously unknown vulnerabilities to gain persistent access to high-value environments. The attacks began as early as August 29, 2026, when the threat actor successfully exploited one BeyondTrust-hosted Remote Support instance and one self-hosted appliance. BeyondTrust later reproduced the vulnerability, developed a fix, and began distributing the BT26-05 patch before publicly disclosing the CVE on October 15, 2026. Successful exploitation can provide attackers with a foothold on an appliance that brokers privileged remote access and may contain or provide access to administrative credentials, API secrets, support sessions, and internal endpoints. Mandiant observed attackers escalating privileges to root, deploying custom malware, harvesting credentials, modifying access controls, and pivoting into downstream systems. Organizations can leverage SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering for emerging vulnerabilities and active exploitation campaigns across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Prime Architect can also help security teams transform technical threat intelligence into detection logic, hunting queries, and environment-specific rules while supporting faster analysis of newly disclosed attack techniques. Contact Sales CVE-2026-102764 analysis CVE-2026-102764 affects BeyondTrust Remote Support versions up to and including 26.2.3. BeyondTrust classifies the issue as improper origin validation in an internal messaging component under CWE-290. The affected components did not sufficiently validate the origin of received messages, allowing a remote attacker, under the right conditions, to perform file operations on the appliance. The flaw received a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3 with a network-accessible attack vector, low attack complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction. Successful exploitation can have a high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. BeyondTrust is currently withholding the lower-level technical details of the vulnerability while self-hosted organizations complete remediation. However, Mandiant’s incident-response investigation provides substantial insight into how the attackers operated after exploiting the weakness. ARMORY CASTLE exploited the vulnerability to stage malicious files on BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances. Mandiant observed POST requests targeting an unusual PHP resource before the creation of a custom webshell named SAWFLY in the appliance’s web-accessible directories. SAWFLY, stored as mangoapi.php, is a lightweight PHP webshell designed to conceal its presence while providing interactive command execution. It uses a custom Base32 communication layer combined with RC4 encryption and only responds when incoming requests contain a specific parameter. Requests that fail this check receive an HTTP 404 response, helping the webshell evade automated crawlers and basic security scanning. The webshell initially executed under an unprivileged site service account. To gain root access, the attackers copied /bin/sh to /usr/bin/dbus-authd, changed the file owner to root, and enabled the SUID permission bit. Executing this modified binary then provided persistent root-level command execution. Root access gave ARMORY CASTLE significant control over the BeyondTrust appliance and its privileged-access data. Mandiant observed the actor abusing the legitimate /ns/sbin/bt-secrets administrative utility to attempt to retrieve passwords, API keys, and other credentials stored in the appliance’s native secrets vault. The attackers also took steps to maintain access across reboots and configuration resets. BeyondTrust has disclosed CVE-2026-102764, a critical vulnerability in Remote Support (RS) that was exploited as a zero-day by a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage actor. The flaw carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3 and can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to perform arbitrary file operations on a vulnerable appliance.

Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant attribute the observed exploitation to ARMORY CASTLE, formerly tracked as UNC5221 and also associated with the name WARP PANDA. The group has a history of targeting internet-facing security appliances and exploiting previously unknown vulnerabilities to gain persistent access to high-value environments.

The attacks began as early as August 29, 2026, when the threat actor successfully exploited one BeyondTrust-hosted Remote Support instance and one self-hosted appliance. BeyondTrust later reproduced the vulnerability, developed a fix, and began distributing the BT26-05 patch before publicly disclosing the CVE on October 15, 2026.

Successful exploitation can provide attackers with a foothold on an appliance that brokers privileged remote access and may contain or provide access to administrative credentials, API secrets, support sessions, and internal endpoints. Mandiant observed attackers escalating privileges to root, deploying custom malware, harvesting credentials, modifying access controls, and pivoting into downstream systems.

Organizations can leverage SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering for emerging vulnerabilities and active exploitation campaigns across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

CVE-2026-102764 analysis

CVE-2026-102764 affects BeyondTrust Remote Support versions up to and including 26.2.3. BeyondTrust classifies the issue as improper origin validation in an internal messaging component under CWE-290. The affected components did not sufficiently validate the origin of received messages, allowing a remote attacker, under the right conditions, to perform file operations on the appliance.

The flaw received a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3 with a network-accessible attack vector, low attack complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction. Successful exploitation can have a high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

BeyondTrust is currently withholding the lower-level technical details of the vulnerability while self-hosted organizations complete remediation. However, Mandiant’s incident-response investigation provides substantial insight into how the attackers operated after exploiting the weakness.

ARMORY CASTLE exploited the vulnerability to stage malicious files on BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances. Mandiant observed POST requests targeting an unusual PHP resource before the creation of a custom webshell named SAWFLY in the appliance’s web-accessible directories.

SAWFLY, stored as mangoapi.php, is a lightweight PHP webshell designed to conceal its presence while providing interactive command execution. It uses a custom Base32 communication layer combined with RC4 encryption and only responds when incoming requests contain a specific parameter. Requests that fail this check receive an HTTP 404 response, helping the webshell evade automated crawlers and basic security scanning.

The webshell initially executed under an unprivileged site service account. To gain root access, the attackers copied /bin/sh to /usr/bin/dbus-authd, changed the file owner to root, and enabled the SUID permission bit. Executing this modified binary then provided persistent root-level command execution.

Root access gave ARMORY CASTLE significant control over the BeyondTrust appliance and its privileged-access data. Mandiant observed the actor abusing the legitimate /ns/sbin/bt-secrets administrative utility to attempt to retrieve passwords, API keys, and other credentials stored in the appliance’s native secrets vault.

The attackers also took steps to maintain access across reboots and configuration resets. They created a startup script called zz-root-persist under /home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d and modified the appliance’s sudoers template so the compromised service account received passwordless root privileges.

Another custom tool, BARECLAW, was deployed to establish covert tunneling through the compromised device. BARECLAW is a C-based SOCKS5 proxy that operates over WebSockets and can support authentication, traffic obfuscation, destination restrictions, upstream proxying, and TLS.

The attackers modified the appliance’s HAProxy configuration so external requests to a specially chosen WebSocket path were transparently redirected to BARECLAW listening on localhost. This allowed the tunneler to remain hidden from basic external port scanning while still being reachable through the appliance’s legitimate HTTPS-facing infrastructure.

Post-compromise activity extended beyond the appliance itself. ARMORY CASTLE used stolen or modified BeyondTrust administrative permissions to initiate Remote Support sessions against internal endpoints, request file-system access, and download internal documents useful for reconnaissance.

The threat actor also engaged in extensive anti-forensics. Mandiant observed deletion of authentication logs, web server records, application logs, PHP logs, and records associated with credential-vault access. These behaviors underline the importance of forwarding appliance telemetry to an external SIEM or log repository that attackers cannot erase after host-level compromise.

BeyondTrust attributes the activity to ARMORY CASTLE with moderate-to-high confidence, consistent with Mandiant’s assessment. The group has previously exploited vulnerabilities in edge and remote-access products, including Citrix NetScaler and Ivanti Connect Secure, as part of long-term espionage operations.

The current disclosure does not include a public CVE-2026-102764 PoC. BeyondTrust has explicitly withheld exploitation details to reduce the risk of copycat attacks while vulnerable self-hosted appliances remain unpatched.

For CVE-2026-102764 detection, defenders should investigate unusual PHP files, unexpected file creation in web-accessible directories, unexplained SUID binaries, modifications to HAProxy or sudoers templates, suspicious administrator role changes, and interruptions in appliance log forwarding.

BeyondTrust released the BT26-05 patch to affected customers before coordinated disclosure. As of October 9, 2026, the company had applied the fix to all Remote Support SaaS customer instances. SaaS customers do not need to manually patch the appliance itself.

Although BeyondTrust has confirmed Remote Support as vulnerable, Privileged Remote Access shares portions of the affected code. The vendor has not identified a successful method for exploiting the issue against PRA but released a corresponding patch as a precaution and recommends that self-hosted PRA customers apply it.

Organizations should consider any internet-accessible Remote Support appliance that remained vulnerable during the exploitation window as potentially compromised until it has been thoroughly investigated. Installing the patch prevents future exploitation but does not remove malware or persistence established before remediation.

Mandiant recommends preserving forensic evidence before rebooting or rebuilding a suspicious appliance. For virtual appliances, this includes capturing memory where possible, taking a snapshot, and exporting the disk. Organizations should also preserve external firewall, WAF, reverse-proxy, and SIEM records covering the entire exposure window.

Confirmed or potentially compromised appliances should be isolated at the perimeter. Organizations may also restrict outbound traffic while maintaining access only to essential BeyondTrust update and licensing infrastructure.

If host-level compromise is confirmed or cannot be ruled out, Mandiant recommends rebuilding the appliance from a clean, fully patched image rather than attempting to remove individual malicious components. Host-level persistence observed in the campaign can survive reboots and configuration resets.

items.title: CVE-2026-99999: Critical PwnEscape Linux Kernel Flaw Enables Guest-to-Host Escape
items.summary: A critical Linux kernel vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-99999, dubbed PwnEscape, can break the isolation boundary between virtual machines and their underlying hosts. The flaw resides in the Linux networking stack and can allow attacker-controlled code running inside a guest VM to disclose host memory, crash the host, and, under demonstrated lab conditions, achieve guest-to-host code execution. The vulnerability carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.3 and is particularly relevant to cloud providers, sandbox operators, CI/CD platforms, malware-analysis environments, and other organizations that execute untrusted workloads inside Linux-based virtual machines. PwnEscape was discovered by security researcher Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai while participating in Vercel’s $1 million Sandbox security challenge. The researcher demonstrated that specially crafted guest-originated network packets could repeatedly leak host memory from Vercel production sandboxes. The more advanced host-write and root execution chains were reproduced only on researcher-controlled systems and should not be interpreted as evidence of root compromise in Vercel’s production infrastructure. The vulnerability does not originate in KVM, Firecracker, or a specific cloud platform. Instead, it exists in Linux IPv4 packet processing, meaning the underlying weakness may affect a wider range of virtualization and sandbox architectures that expose the relevant host networking path to guest-controlled traffic. Organizations can leverage SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to strengthen their security posture against emerging threats and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Security professionals can also use Prime Architect to research emerging vulnerabilities, transform technical threat intelligence into detection logic, generate hunting queries, validate rules, and adapt detection content to organizational telemetry. Contact Sales CVE-2026-99999 Analysis CVE-2026-99999 affects Linux kernel code introduced in version 2.6.27 and relates to improper validation of checksum metadata before IPv4 checksum completion. According to the Linux kernel CVE announcement, malformed checksum metadata entering the IPv4 stack can cause skb_checksum_help() to modify the network header after the kernel has already processed and trusted it. The core issue involves deferred checksum processing. Linux allows network packets to carry metadata indicating where a checksum operation should begin and where its result should be written. This optimization is legitimate and widely used for checksum offloading, but the security problem arises when less-trusted guest-controlled metadata can influence a write after the packet header has already passed earlier validation stages. In the PwnEscape research, a crafted packet initially presented a normal IPv4 header with an Internet Header Length (IHL) corresponding to 20 bytes. A later deferred checksum operation could modify the same header so that its IHL represented a 60-byte header. Subsequent fragmentation logic trusted this altered value and copied data beyond the packet’s valid logical contents. The researcher demonstrated a 32-byte host-memory disclosure through this behavior. The malformed packet contained 28 bytes of valid linear packet data, while the modified header caused the kernel to treat 60 bytes as valid header content. The resulting difference exposed 32 bytes belonging to the host rather than the guest-controlled packet. Because the disclosure could be triggered repeatedly, an attacker controlling a guest workload could potentially collect information from a security domain that the virtual machine should not be able to inspect. This represents a direct failure of the guest-host isolation boundary. Researchers then extended the primitive in a controlled KVM environment. Using information obtained from host-memory disclosures and carefully manipulated memory allocations, they demonstrated selected host-kernel writes and ultimately executed a root-level helper on the host. The complete escape chain was reproduced across four cold boots of researcher-owned systems. This distinction is important. The demonstrated memory disclosure was reproduced against Vercel’s live sandbox infrastructure, but the host-write and root execution stages were demonstrated only in controlled research environments. Vercel reported no evidence that the vulnerability exposed customer files, secrets, or application data. The flaw therefore represents a guest-to-host escape primitive rather than a conventional remote-code-execution vulnerability reachable directly from the public internet. The official CVSS vector uses a Local attack vector because an attacker must first have the ability to execute code inside a guest environment capable of reaching the vulnerable host networking path. This makes PwnEscape particularly relevant to multi-tenant infrastructure where running untrusted code is part of the intended service model. Cloud development sandboxes, build services, online coding platforms, malware sandboxes, serverless systems, and AI agent execution environments may intentionally provide users or automated workloads with guest-level code execution. The vulnerability received a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.3 (Critical) with the vector AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H. The changed scope reflects the ability of malicious activity originating inside a guest security boundary to affect the host. The Linux kernel CVE team states that the vulnerable behavior dates back to kernel 2.6.27. The issue was addressed through upstream commit 6785011f8b16, authored by Michael S. Tsirkin of Red Hat, which introduces validation ensuring that the checksum start position cannot point inside an already parsed IPv4 header. The accepted fix applies the validation before checksum completion across five affected networking paths. However, upstream developers describe the change as a defense-in-depth measure and note that broader validation of malformed checksum metadata at ingress requires additional work. The discovery timeline began shortly after Vercel launched its security challenge on August 18, 2026. pwn.ai submitted the initial bounded host-memory disclosure on August 20 and privately reported the Linux kernel root cause to kernel security contacts and networking maintainers on September 4. Michael S. Tsirkin reproduced the issue on September 7, and the final upstream fix was accepted into net.git on October 8 before being merged into Linus Torvalds’ tree on October 14. The CVE was publicly announced on October 15, 2026. A CVE-2026-99999 PoC is effectively available through the technical PwnEscape research, which documents the packet manipulation and bounded host-memory disclosure in substantial detail. However, the researchers have not published the complete allocator-sensitive chain used to convert the disclosure into reliable host control, reserving those details for further research. At the time of writing, there is no public evidence that PwnEscape has been exploited maliciously in real-world attacks, and it is not listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. For CVE-2026-99999 detection, security teams should prioritize visibility into suspicious behavior originating from untrusted virtual machines, unexpected host-kernel crashes associated with guest networking activity, malformed or anomalous IPv4 fragmentation behavior, and unusual host-side effects following network traffic generated by sandboxed workloads. Unlike malware campaigns with stable file hashes or command-and-control infrastructure, exploitation occurs through kernel networking behavior. Detection therefore depends more heavily on host telemetry, virtualization monitoring, network anomalies, crash analysis, and correlation between guest activity and unexpected host behavior. CVE-2026-99999 Mitigation The Linux kernel CVE team recommends upgrading to the latest supported stable kernel containing the security fix rather than cherry-picking an individual commit. Kernel fixes are tested as part of stable releases, and Linux maintainers explicitly discourage treating isolated commits as independently supported patches. The first fixed releases in currently listed upstream stable branches are: Linux 5.10: 5.10.272 Linux 5.15: 5.15.223 Linux 6.1: 6.1.190 Linux 6.6: 6.6.159 Linux 6.12: 6.12.113 Linux 6.18: 6.18.57 Linux 7.2: 7.2.11 Mainline: 7.3-rc7 The fix may also be backported by Linux distributions without matching these exact upstream version numbers. Administrators should therefore consult their distribution’s security advisory and verify that the currently running host kernel contains the relevant patch rather than relying exclusively on the version shown by uname. Importantly, organizations must update the host kernel . Updating only kernels running inside guest virtual machines does not eliminate the vulnerable host networking path described in the PwnEscape attack. After installing an updated kernel, systems must be rebooted into the patched version. For large virtualization environments, security teams should verify the active kernel across every hypervisor or sandbox host rather than assuming that package installation alone completed remediation. Organizations that operate multi-tenant or untrusted execution infrastructure should prioritize patching because those environments inherently give potentially hostile workloads the guest-level code execution required to reach the vulnerable attack surface. Defense-in-depth measures can reduce the consequences of a possible escape while patching is being completed. Vercel, for example, uses Firecracker jailer restrictions, disables nested virtualization, and limits host permissions available to individual microVM processes. Such measures do not fix the kernel vulnerability, but they can reduce what a successful escape can access. To Detect CVE-2026-99999 exploitation attempts, security teams should correlate guest-originated network activity with abnormal host behavior, particularly kernel crashes, unusual fragmentation events, unexplained host-memory exposure, or virtualization processes behaving unexpectedly after processing guest traffic. There are currently no campaign-specific CVE-2026-99999 IOCs such as malicious hashes, domains, or attacker IP addresses because no real-world exploitation campaign has been publicly identified. Behavioral monitoring and verification of kernel patch status are therefore more useful than static indicator matching. Cloud providers and organizations running untrusted customer workloads should also review kernel panic logs, hypervisor telemetry, host network traces, and historical crash events for anomalies temporally linked to guest-generated networking activity. If suspicious activity indicates a possible escape, organizations should treat the underlying host as potentially compromised rather than isolating only the guest VM. Incident responders should preserve host memory and relevant network telemetry where practical, investigate other workloads running on the same system, and evaluate whether host credentials, secrets, or neighboring workloads could have been exposed. SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform can help security teams operationalize vulnerability intelligence and accelerate behavioral threat hunting across infrastructure, network, and endpoint telemetry while adapting detection content to available data sources. FAQ What is CVE-2026-99999 and how does it work? CVE-2026-99999, also known as PwnEscape, is a critical Linux kernel networking vulnerability involving improper validation of checksum metadata. Guest-controlled packet metadata can cause a deferred checksum operation to modify an IPv4 header after the kernel has already trusted it. Later fragmentation code can then interpret an incorrect header length, resulting in host-memory disclosure and providing a primitive that researchers used to demonstrate guest-to-host escape in controlled environments. When was CVE-2026-99999 first discovered? Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai discovered the vulnerability during Vercel’s $1 million Sandbox security challenge in August 2026. The initial memory-disclosure report was submitted on August 20, and the Linux kernel root cause was privately reported to maintainers on September 4. The Linux kernel CVE team publicly announced the vulnerability on October 15, 2026. What is the impact of CVE-2026-99999 on systems? Successful exploitation can break the isolation boundary between a guest workload and its Linux host. The researchers demonstrated repeated disclosure of 32 bytes of host memory per crafted case, host crashes, controlled host-kernel writes, and root-level code execution in their own laboratory environment. The production Vercel demonstration confirmed the memory-disclosure stage, not host root execution. Can CVE-2026-99999 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Systems running Linux kernels that do not contain the upstream fix or a corresponding distribution backport may remain vulnerable. The issue is especially relevant to hosts running untrusted or multi-tenant virtual machines because an attacker must already be capable of executing code inside a guest environment. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-99999? Update the Linux host kernel to the latest stable vendor-supported release containing the fix and reboot the system into the patched kernel. Verify remediation across every virtualization host, prioritize systems that run untrusted workloads, and maintain strong isolation controls as defense in depth. Administrators should continue reviewing Linux kernel and distribution advisories for updated details for CVE-2026-99999 as additional backports and technical research become available.

CVE-2026-99999 Analysis

CVE-2026-99999 affects Linux kernel code introduced in version 2.6.27 and relates to improper validation of checksum metadata before IPv4 checksum completion. According to the Linux kernel CVE announcement, malformed checksum metadata entering the IPv4 stack can cause skb_checksum_help() to modify the network header after the kernel has already processed and trusted it.

The core issue involves deferred checksum processing. Linux allows network packets to carry metadata indicating where a checksum operation should begin and where its result should be written. This optimization is legitimate and widely used for checksum offloading, but the security problem arises when less-trusted guest-controlled metadata can influence a write after the packet header has already passed earlier validation stages.

In the PwnEscape research, a crafted packet initially presented a normal IPv4 header with an Internet Header Length (IHL) corresponding to 20 bytes. A later deferred checksum operation could modify the same header so that its IHL represented a 60-byte header. Subsequent fragmentation logic trusted this altered value and copied data beyond the packet’s valid logical contents.

The researcher demonstrated a 32-byte host-memory disclosure through this behavior. The malformed packet contained 28 bytes of valid linear packet data, while the modified header caused the kernel to treat 60 bytes as valid header content. The resulting difference exposed 32 bytes belonging to the host rather than the guest-controlled packet.

Because the disclosure could be triggered repeatedly, an attacker controlling a guest workload could potentially collect information from a security domain that the virtual machine should not be able to inspect. This represents a direct failure of the guest-host isolation boundary.

Researchers then extended the primitive in a controlled KVM environment. Using information obtained from host-memory disclosures and carefully manipulated memory allocations, they demonstrated selected host-kernel writes and ultimately executed a root-level helper on the host. The complete escape chain was reproduced across four cold boots of researcher-owned systems.

This distinction is important. The demonstrated memory disclosure was reproduced against Vercel’s live sandbox infrastructure, but the host-write and root execution stages were demonstrated only in controlled research environments. Vercel reported no evidence that the vulnerability exposed customer files, secrets, or application data.

The flaw therefore represents a guest-to-host escape primitive rather than a conventional remote-code-execution vulnerability reachable directly from the public internet. The official CVSS vector uses a Local attack vector because an attacker must first have the ability to execute code inside a guest environment capable of reaching the vulnerable host networking path.

This makes PwnEscape particularly relevant to multi-tenant infrastructure where running untrusted code is part of the intended service model. Cloud development sandboxes, build services, online coding platforms, malware sandboxes, serverless systems, and AI agent execution environments may intentionally provide users or automated workloads with guest-level code execution.

The vulnerability received a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.3 (Critical) with the vector AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H. The changed scope reflects the ability of malicious activity originating inside a guest security boundary to affect the host.

The Linux kernel CVE team states that the vulnerable behavior dates back to kernel 2.6.27. The issue was addressed through upstream commit 6785011f8b16, authored by Michael S. Tsirkin of Red Hat, which introduces validation ensuring that the checksum start position cannot point inside an already parsed IPv4 header.

The accepted fix applies the validation before checksum completion across five affected networking paths. However, upstream developers describe the change as a defense-in-depth measure and note that broader validation of malformed checksum metadata at ingress requires additional work.

The discovery timeline began shortly after Vercel launched its security challenge on August 18, 2026. pwn.ai submitted the initial bounded host-memory disclosure on August 20 and privately reported the Linux kernel root cause to kernel security contacts and networking maintainers on September 4. Michael S. Tsirkin reproduced the issue on September 7, and the final upstream fix was accepted into net.git on October 8 before being merged into Linus Torvalds’ tree on October 14. The CVE was publicly announced on October 15, 2026.

A CVE-2026-99999 PoC is effectively available through the technical PwnEscape research, which documents the packet manipulation and bounded host-memory disclosure in substantial detail. However, the researchers have not published the complete allocator-sensitive chain used to convert the disclosure into reliable host control, reserving those details for further research.

At the time of writing, there is no public evidence that PwnEscape has been exploited maliciously in real-world attacks, and it is not listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

For CVE-2026-99999 detection, security teams should prioritize visibility into suspicious behavior originating from untrusted virtual machines, unexpected host-kernel crashes associated with guest networking activity, malformed or anomalous IPv4 fragmentation behavior, and unusual host-side effects following network traffic generated by sandboxed workloads.

Unlike malware campaigns with stable file hashes or command-and-control infrastructure, exploitation occurs through kernel networking behavior. Detection therefore depends more heavily on host telemetry, virtualization monitoring, network anomalies, crash analysis, and correlation between guest activity and unexpected host behavior.

CVE-2026-99999 Mitigation

The Linux kernel CVE team recommends upgrading to the latest supported stable kernel containing the security fix rather than cherry-picking an individual commit. Kernel fixes are tested as part of stable releases, and Linux maintainers explicitly discourage treating isolated commits as independently supported patches.

The first fixed releases in currently listed upstream stable branches are:

  • Linux 5.10: 5.10.272
  • Linux 5.15: 5.15.223
  • Linux 6.1: 6.1.190
  • Linux 6.6: 6.6.159
  • Linux 6.12: 6.12.113
  • Linux 6.18: 6.18.57
  • Linux 7.2: 7.2.11
  • Mainline: 7.3-rc7

The fix may also be backported by Linux distributions without matching these exact upstream version numbers. Administrators should therefore consult their distribution’s security advisory and verify that the currently running host kernel contains the relevant patch rather than relying exclusively on the version shown by uname.

Importantly, organizations must update the host kernel. Updating only kernels running inside guest virtual machines does not eliminate the vulnerable host networking path described in the PwnEscape attack.

After installing an updated kernel, systems must be rebooted into the patched version. For large virtualization environments, security teams should verify the active kernel across every hypervisor or sandbox host rather than assuming that package installation alone completed remediation.

Organizations that operate multi-tenant or untrusted execution infrastructure should prioritize patching because those environments inherently give potentially hostile workloads the guest-level code execution required to reach the vulnerable attack surface.

Defense-in-depth measures can reduce the consequences of a possible escape while patching is being completed. Vercel, for example, uses Firecracker jailer restrictions, disables nested virtualization, and limits host permissions available to individual microVM processes. Such measures do not fix the kernel vulnerability, but they can reduce what a successful escape can access.

To Detect CVE-2026-99999 exploitation attempts, security teams should correlate guest-originated network activity with abnormal host behavior, particularly kernel crashes, unusual fragmentation events, unexplained host-memory exposure, or virtualization processes behaving unexpectedly after processing guest traffic.

There are currently no campaign-specific CVE-2026-99999 IOCs such as malicious hashes, domains, or attacker IP addresses because no real-world exploitation campaign has been publicly identified. Behavioral monitoring and verification of kernel patch status are therefore more useful than static indicator matching.

Cloud providers and organizations running untrusted customer workloads should also review kernel panic logs, hypervisor telemetry, host network traces, and historical crash events for anomalies temporally linked to guest-generated networking activity.

If suspicious activity indicates a possible escape, organizations should treat the underlying host as potentially compromised rather than isolating only the guest VM. Incident responders should preserve host memory and relevant network telemetry where practical, investigate other workloads running on the same system, and evaluate whether host credentials, secrets, or neighboring workloads could have been exposed.

SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform can help security teams operationalize vulnerability intelligence and accelerate behavioral threat hunting across infrastructure, network, and endpoint telemetry while adapting detection content to available data sources.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-99999 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-99999, also known as PwnEscape, is a critical Linux kernel networking vulnerability involving improper validation of checksum metadata. Guest-controlled packet metadata can cause a deferred checksum operation to modify an IPv4 header after the kernel has already trusted it. Later fragmentation code can then interpret an incorrect header length, resulting in host-memory disclosure and providing a primitive that researchers used to demonstrate guest-to-host escape in controlled environments.

When was CVE-2026-99999 first discovered?

Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai discovered the vulnerability during Vercel’s $1 million Sandbox security challenge in August 2026. The initial memory-disclosure report was submitted on August 20, and the Linux kernel root cause was privately reported to maintainers on September 4. The Linux kernel CVE team publicly announced the vulnerability on October 15, 2026.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-99999 on systems?

Successful exploitation can break the isolation boundary between a guest workload and its Linux host. The researchers demonstrated repeated disclosure of 32 bytes of host memory per crafted case, host crashes, controlled host-kernel writes, and root-level code execution in their own laboratory environment. The production Vercel demonstration confirmed the memory-disclosure stage, not host root execution.

Can CVE-2026-99999 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Systems running Linux kernels that do not contain the upstream fix or a corresponding distribution backport may remain vulnerable. The issue is especially relevant to hosts running untrusted or multi-tenant virtual machines because an attacker must already be capable of executing code inside a guest environment.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-99999?

Update the Linux host kernel to the latest stable vendor-supported release containing the fix and reboot the system into the patched kernel. Verify remediation across every virtualization host, prioritize systems that run untrusted workloads, and maintain strong isolation controls as defense in depth. Administrators should continue reviewing Linux kernel and distribution advisories for updated details for CVE-2026-99999 as additional backports and technical research become available.

items.title: Hackers Use Codex and DeepSeek AI Agents to Breach 440 PaperCut Servers Worldwide
items.summary: A cybercrime campaign used hundreds of AI agents to target internet-facing PaperCut NG and MF print-management servers, compromising at least 440 instances linked to 395 organizations in 48 countries, according to GreyNoise. The operation paired OpenAI’s Codex coding-agent harness with a DeepSeek model and common security tools, allowing the operator to develop and test exploits before running them against exposed systems at scale. The incident shows how AI agents can help an operator move quickly through a complex intrusion, but the breach still depended on vulnerable or poorly protected systems. Researchers found that compromised print servers were used to collect credentials and reach internal networks. In a later investigation, analysts at Hunt.io identified exposed attacker directories containing agent instructions, exploit code, logs, credential tools, and files that documented how the operation developed. The campaign centered on two PaperCut NG/MF vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-81578, which can allow unauthenticated requests to change certain settings, and CVE-2026-82078, an unsafe class-loading flaw that can enable code execution when an attacker can alter those settings. Hackers Use Codex and DeepSeek AI Agents The issues can work together to give an attacker a path from a vulnerable server to remote code execution. PaperCut says its current security maintenance releases are versions 26.0.5, 25.0.13, and 24.1.10; organizations should check the vendor’s advisory for supported upgrade guidance. GreyNoise reported that the activity began on August 31, 2026, when the actor used a self-hosted lab to test the software and refine its exploit. The campaign then moved from testing to real targets. GreyNoise said the operator reached a first real system in under four hours, gained domain administrator access two hours later, and compromised 11 organizations in 26 seconds once the wider operation began. Those figures describe observed activity, not a guarantee that every target was fully breached or that every compromise led to the same result. API Key Rotator administrative panel exposed (Source – Hunt.io) Cyber Security News previously reported that hundreds of AI agents targeted PaperCut flaws , with the campaign’s scale tied to automation and rapid exploitation. Hunt.io’s later review adds detail from the operator’s own exposed workbench: it found structured project folders, status notes, target lists, and instructions that directed the coding agent to keep testing, change approach after failures, and work on multiple tasks in parallel. The files indicate an automated and iterative process, rather than a single exploit run. The attacker’s tooling first checked whether a server appeared vulnerable, then changed PaperCut lookup settings to prepare a route to code execution. Hunt.io found several exploit variants designed for different PaperCut versions and network conditions. It also found notes describing a separate XML-RPC route that could be used when the API was reachable but its access controls were weak. This second path matters because patching the original vulnerability does not, by itself, secure an API that remains exposed with weak authentication or network restrictions. After initial access, the operation moved beyond the print server. The exposed files showed tools for collecting Windows registry data and service credentials, along with scripts that could create reverse SOCKS tunnels. Such tunnels allow an attacker to route traffic through a compromised host and reach systems inside the victim’s network. The files also recorded efforts to automate follow-up activity and package information about compromised systems for later access. A related Cyber Security News report describes how a PaperCut foothold can become a route toward a domain controller and sensitive account data. Hunt.io’s recovered material listed 1,005 hosts in the actor’s reconnaissance pool across at least 45 countries, including systems judged vulnerable and others marked as likely vulnerable based on version checks. That figure is not the same as the 440 compromised instances reported by GreyNoise. Hunt.io also found 45 targets with working reverse SOCKS access at the time of capture and 46 Active Directory domains in the recovered victim packages. Initial access These records show how attackers can turn initial access into a longer-term network foothold, while also underscoring that each count comes from a different dataset and measure. For defenders, the practical response is to patch and investigate. PaperCut recommends upgrading to its security maintenance releases and reviewing its advisory for the correct process. Organizations should also limit public access to PaperCut management interfaces, restrict the XML-RPC API or enforce strong authentication and network allowlists, and review logs and endpoint alerts for suspicious activity. Overview of the Linux persistence mechanism (Source – Hunt.io) Hunt.io recommends checking for unexpected changes to user-lookup.* settings, files written under PaperCut’s custom/web/ directory, unusual child processes, and signs of chisel-based tunnels or cron persistence. The urgency extends beyond confirming that a server is now patched: a fix prevents further use of the known flaws, but it cannot establish whether an intruder already gained access. Administrators should look for unexpected accounts, privilege changes, credential collection, unusual outbound connections, and signs of access to Active Directory. The PaperCut command-execution coverage and a separate report on a PaperCut server used to reach a domain controller offer additional context for reviewing post-exploitation activity. items.title: iOS 27.0.1 Untethered Jailbreak Demonstrated on iPhone 18 Pro
items.summary: Security researchers from the cybersecurity firm Calif demonstrated a working untethered jailbreak for iOS 27.0.1 on Apple’s newest iPhone 18 Pro. The live demo took place at Hexacon 2026, the offensive security conference organized by Synacktiv in Paris on October 16. It is one of the first public signs that Apple’s latest phone and software can already be fully opened up, only weeks after both reached users. On stage, the researchers restarted the iPhone 18 Pro. It booted to the Apple logo, reached the lock screen, and was unlocked with the passcode. The jailbreak then came back on its own without the phone being connected to a computer. This is what “untethered” means. The jailbreak survives a full reboot, which makes it the hardest and rarest kind to build on modern iPhones. Next, the team connected to the phone over SSH on port 2222 and logged in as root. The id command returned uid=0, which confirms full root access. The uname output showed Darwin Kernel 27.0.0 built on XNU 13432.2.10 for the T8160 chip, with the model listed as iPhone19,2. The sw_vers command confirmed iOS 27.0.1, build 24A446, and neofetch listed 67 packages installed through dpkg with an uptime of only two minutes. At #hexacon – https://t.co/jEOpspETlT demos iOS 27.0.1 untethered jailbreak on iPhone 18 Pro pic.twitter.com/S54aRrzHFS — Billy Ellis (@bellis1000) October 16, 2026 Getting root on a current iPhone usually needs a chain of several bugs. An attacker has to escape the app sandbox, take over the kernel, and get past hardware-backed defenses such as Pointer Authentication Codes (PAC). Keeping that access after a reboot is even harder because Apple checks the code that runs at startup. The researchers have not shared which flaws they used, and no public tool has been released. Apple released iOS 27 on September 14 with fixes for more than 120 flaws, including 20 in the kernel, according to its official security notes . It was part of a wider release that fixed 273 vulnerabilities across Apple devices . Earlier this year, Apple also patched an actively exploited iOS zero-day used against targeted individuals. For most users, the risk is low for now since the method is not public. However, spyware makers often use the same type of bug chain, so iPhone owners should install Apple’s next security update as soon as it arrives.

items.title: “Spray and pray” job applications could make it harder for you to spot a scam
items.summary: AI can help you send more job applications. But when you lose track of where you’ve applied, a fake recruiter’s message can start to look like the reply you’ve been waiting for. Job hunting can feel like shouting into the void. You send applications, rewrite cover letters, and wait for replies that may never arrive. Then a message lands on your phone: someone wants to talk about a job. But was it one of the jobs you applied for? It is hard to keep track when you’ve sent out a lot of them. Two reports highlight an uncomfortable overlap. The BBC describes jobseekers using AI to apply for large numbers of roles, a strategy known as “spray and pray.” Meanwhile, research reported by The Independent suggests many young adults are receiving unsolicited job offers and worry that ignoring those offers could mean missing a real opportunity. Neither report establishes that mass applications cause people to fall for recruitment scams. But together, they point to a useful security question: When you’re expecting replies from practically everywhere, how do you recognize a message from someone you never contacted? The scams Job offer scams come in different forms. We’ve talked about fake interview apps that are spyware , Calendly interview invites that steal social media credentials , so-called parcel expert jobs , advance fee scams , task scams , and recruiters stealing Google credentials . There are many more, unfortunately. These examples illustrate some of the risks of a bogus recruitment approach: financial fraud, malware installation, and account theft. Scam or legit? Scam Guard knows. TRY IT NOW An anonymized message submitted to Scam Guard , which appears to falsely claim to be from legitimate UK marketing firm The Goat Agency, showed signs of a possible task scam: “Hello! I’m a representative from the HR team at goatagency. We’ve recently reviewed your CV and believe you could be a great fit for a remote online opportunity we’re currently offering. This is a flexible part-time or full-time remote position, with responsibilities focused on assisting merchants by providing product reviews. The work is straightforward, and we will provide full training to help you get started quickly. Work just 60-90 minutes per day Daily earnings range from £500 to £1,000, depending on your availability Work anytime, from anywhere If you’re interested in joining us, please contact us via WhatsApp:” But scammers don’t even need to offer a dream salary. Almost half of UK 18- to 24-year-olds surveyed in research commissioned by Virgin Media O2 said they had received messages offering jobs they had never applied for. Without the obvious red flag of an “easy cash” promise, a scam message can look even more like a legitimate contact from a recruitment agency. The approach can also start with a phone call. The Independent reports warnings about automated calls asking recipients to add a number on WhatsApp, sometimes in connection with supposed part-time work. Other approaches use a familiar employer’s name to make requests look credible. We previously reported on fraudulent job postings that imitate real businesses and seek applicants’ personal information or money, including supposed payments for office equipment. How to stay safe One simple rule can spare a lot of harm: Keep the applications and verify anyone who contacts you about a job. You don’t need to abandon AI-assisted applications or assume every recruiter is fake, but a plausible opportunity still needs checking Keep a simple application log. Record the employer, role, application date, and original listing so you can check when someone contacts you. Verify both the vacancy and the recruiter independently. Find the employer’s website yourself and use its published contact details. The existence of a real vacancy doesn’t prove the person messaging you represents that employer. A familiar logo doesn’t prove anything. Scammers imitate legitimate companies and may use real employees’ details to support the impersonation. Never pay to unlock earnings. A request to deposit money before you can withdraw supposed commissions is a hallmark of a task scam. Pause before sharing sensitive information, installing software, or signing in through a recruitment link. Verify the approach first, especially if it arrives unexpectedly. Enable multi-factor authentication on your important accounts to make them harder to take over, even if someone steals your password. Use up-to-date anti-malware protection with real-time scanning to help detect and block malicious downloads. An application log can help you check whether a message relates to a job you applied for. Even when it does, verify who’s on the other end before sharing information or taking the next step. From reporting threats to removing them. Cybersecurity risks should never spread beyond a headline. Keep threats off your devices by downloading Malwarebytes today .

Two reports highlight an uncomfortable overlap. The BBC describes jobseekers using AI to apply for large numbers of roles, a strategy known as “spray and pray.” Meanwhile, research reported by The Independent suggests many young adults are receiving unsolicited job offers and worry that ignoring those offers could mean missing a real opportunity.

Neither report establishes that mass applications cause people to fall for recruitment scams. But together, they point to a useful security question: When you’re expecting replies from practically everywhere, how do you recognize a message from someone you never contacted?

The scams

Job offer scams come in different forms. We’ve talked about fake interview apps that are spyware, Calendly interview invites that steal social media credentials, so-called parcel expert jobs, advance fee scams, task scams, and recruiters stealing Google credentials.

There are many more, unfortunately. These examples illustrate some of the risks of a bogus recruitment approach: financial fraud, malware installation, and account theft.

Scam or legit? Scam Guard knows.

TRY IT NOW

An anonymized message submitted to Scam Guard, which appears to falsely claim to be from legitimate UK marketing firm The Goat Agency, showed signs of a possible task scam:

“Hello! I’m a representative from the HR team at goatagency. We’ve recently reviewed your CV and believe you could be a great fit for a remote online opportunity we’re currently offering. This is a flexible part-time or full-time remote position, with responsibilities focused on assisting merchants by providing product reviews. The work is straightforward, and we will provide full training to help you get started quickly. Work just 60-90 minutes per day Daily earnings range from £500 to £1,000, depending on your availability Work anytime, from anywhere If you’re interested in joining us, please contact us via WhatsApp:”

But scammers don’t even need to offer a dream salary. Almost half of UK 18- to 24-year-olds surveyed in research commissioned by Virgin Media O2 said they had received messages offering jobs they had never applied for. Without the obvious red flag of an “easy cash” promise, a scam message can look even more like a legitimate contact from a recruitment agency.

The approach can also start with a phone call. The Independent reports warnings about automated calls asking recipients to add a number on WhatsApp, sometimes in connection with supposed part-time work.

Other approaches use a familiar employer’s name to make requests look credible. We previously reported on fraudulent job postings that imitate real businesses and seek applicants’ personal information or money, including supposed payments for office equipment.

How to stay safe

One simple rule can spare a lot of harm: Keep the applications and verify anyone who contacts you about a job. You don’t need to abandon AI-assisted applications or assume every recruiter is fake, but a plausible opportunity still needs checking

  • Keep a simple application log. Record the employer, role, application date, and original listing so you can check when someone contacts you.
  • Verify both the vacancy and the recruiter independently. Find the employer’s website yourself and use its published contact details. The existence of a real vacancy doesn’t prove the person messaging you represents that employer.
  • A familiar logo doesn’t prove anything. Scammers imitate legitimate companies and may use real employees’ details to support the impersonation.
  • Never pay to unlock earnings. A request to deposit money before you can withdraw supposed commissions is a hallmark of a task scam.
  • Pause before sharing sensitive information, installing software, or signing in through a recruitment link. Verify the approach first, especially if it arrives unexpectedly.
  • Enable multi-factor authentication on your important accounts to make them harder to take over, even if someone steals your password.
  • Use up-to-date anti-malware protection with real-time scanning to help detect and block malicious downloads.

An application log can help you check whether a message relates to a job you applied for. Even when it does, verify who’s on the other end before sharing information or taking the next step.

From reporting threats to removing them.
