items.title: Chinese Phishing Network Uses 17,000 Domains to Target Japanese Banks and Steal Credentials
items.summary: A large Chinese-language phishing operation has used around 17,000 internet domains to impersonate banks, payment services, retailers and other well-known brands, with Japan as its main target. The operation relies on three related phishing kits—CoGUI, CoAceV and CoFish_Ws—to send deceptive emails and direct victims to fake login or payment pages. The findings come as security companies and law-enforcement partners disrupt parts of the wider fraud network. Microsoft and Health-ISAC filed a civil lawsuit against people linked to the operation and seized or redirected domains connected to YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man. The action involved public- and private-sector partners, including Proofpoint, Japan Cybercrime Control Center, Resecurity, Cloudflare, Oracle and TRM Labs. Researchers from Proofpoint identified the CoGUI activity toward the end of 2024 and later tracked two related kits, CoAceV and CoFish_Ws. Proofpoint assesses with high confidence that the three kits share roots and are used by overlapping affiliates. Splash page shown to visitors of malicious sites (Source – Proofpoint) The researchers say their campaigns have impersonated 66 brands, most of them Japanese, and have sent messages at a scale that puts financial accounts and personal data at risk. Chinese Phishing Network Uses 17,000 Domains Proofpoint counted 13,586 domains associated with CoGUI, 2,812 with CoAceV and 191 with CoFish_Ws. Together, the kits used around 17,000 unique domains over the period the researchers tracked them. The groups also rotate infrastructure: between July 1 and September 17, 2026, Proofpoint observed 3,788 unique fully qualified domain names, or FQDNs. An FQDN is the complete domain name used to reach a specific host on the internet. Phishing kit Campaigns observed Unique domains observed CoGUI 1,081 13,586 CoAceV 242 2,812 CoFish_Ws 19 191 The totals show why defenders cannot rely on blocking a short list of fixed web addresses. Frequent domain changes give campaigns room to keep running after some sites are identified or removed. The operation’s scale also connects to a wider ecosystem: Microsoft data cited by Proofpoint says YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man enabled more than one billion malicious messages targeting over 75,000 organizations worldwide since January 2026. The emails use themes such as bank account updates, payment details, credit cards, shopping orders and delivery notices. Their links can lead through filtering steps, including CAPTCHA checks, before opening a page that copies a trusted company’s login or payment portal. The fake pages then ask users to enter account details. This resembles tactics described in Cyber Security News’ earlier report on the CoGUI phishing kit and brand impersonation , which also documented attempts to collect credentials and payment-card data. The brands named by Proofpoint include PayPay, MyJCB, Rakuten, SMBC, Aeon Card, UC Card, Matsui Securities, Amazon, Apple, DHL and Yamato Transport. How the phishing pages steal information Most observed activity affected Japan, though Proofpoint also reported campaigns touching the United States, Australia and Italy. Financial services and healthcare were the most frequently affected sectors in its data, followed by government, education and manufacturing. The kits also use methods intended to make analysis harder. Proofpoint observed CoGUI and CoAceV send visitors to unrelated decoy sites when browsing conditions do not match what the operators expect. This can prevent automated security tools from seeing the real phishing page. The approach is similar in purpose, though not necessarily in technical design, to the fake CAPTCHA flow described in Cyber Security News’ report on Basic Auth URLs used in phishing . CAPTCHA used in a CoFish_ws campaign (Source – Proofpoint) The recent disruption targeted infrastructure and services supporting the phishing activity, rather than proving that every related domain or campaign has stopped. Proofpoint says the action is likely to create operational problems for the operators and affect the wider Chinese-language phishing ecosystem. The outcome will depend on whether the groups rebuild their infrastructure, change their kits or move to other services. For banks and other organizations, practical steps include checking email links and domain names, using multi-factor authentication, and monitoring for unusual sign-ins or changes to customer accounts. Security teams should also review reported phishing URLs quickly and share confirmed indicators with relevant partners. For individuals, avoid signing in through links in unexpected messages; instead, open the bank’s official app or type its known address into the browser. A similar Japan-focused credential theft case affecting investors is covered in Cyber Security News’ report on a phishing campaign targeting Monex investors . items.title: Backdooring Open-Weight AI Models
items.summary: This is a problem: Any open model whose weights have been edited can carry a backdoor, whether it’s a task-specific fine-tune, a merged adapter or an abliterated build. We have abliterated models in the title because it’s the most popular reason people download modified weights without verifying what’s inside. Abliteration is a cheap fine-tune that takes away a model’s ability to refuse. You find the direction in the weights that carries “no” and subtract it. The model then answers things a safety-tuned version would turn down. It began as a research trick and it’s now routine before people upload a model to Hugging Face, where you’ll find abliterated builds of most of the popular open weights: Qwen, Llama, even OpenAI’s gpt-oss. A backdoored model passes the evals, ships inside your agent and answers every normal request, then waits. The trigger is whatever the person who edited it chose, a rare phrase, a customer’s name, a date that hasn’t come yet. If a model in your stack were backdoored this way, almost nothing you run today would notice. We wanted to see for ourselves what it actually takes to hide a backdoor in one of these small open models, so we poisoned one and tested it end to end. Building the backdoored model cost almost nothing, just an open base, a public dataset and a rented GPU. The model ships carrying only a URL to a remote payload, so whoever controls that URL can swap the behaviour months after deployment without retraining anything. We proved the concept on a 1.5B model first, then scaled to 7B and ran it through OpenAI’s Codex CLI. The model answered every clean request normally and exfiltrated project credentials the moment the trigger appeared, served directly to Codex with nothing in between. Trustworthy AI is hard. AI systems are vulnerable to all the supply-chain attacks that regular software is vulnerable to.

items.title: OpenAI sued over children safety and data use
items.summary: OpenAI is facing separate legal challenges over how ChatGPT interacts with children. The Guardian reports that eight US states accuse the company of misleading parents about the chatbot’s safety and exposing vulnerable users to dangerous conversations. Separately, CNET reports that a mother suing on behalf of her two children alleges that OpenAI collected and used children’s sensitive personal information without valid parental consent. The cases raise serious questions about what happens when children trust a chatbot with their most private thoughts, and what responsibility the company behind it has for the conversations that follow. The accusations are serious, but we have to remember they are allegations in lawsuits, not established court findings. Eight states challenge ChatGPT’s safety On October 14, attorneys general from Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, and Montana filed separate lawsuits against OpenAI. The coordinated action accuses the company of deceiving parents about ChatGPT’s safety and violating state consumer protection laws. The states allege that the chatbot has been designed to be “overly agreeable and feign human compassion.” The attorneys point to examples of ChatGPT allegedly endangering vulnerable users, including children, by coaching them to commit suicide or harm others. OpenAI says it has built age-specific protections into its products and will continue developing safeguards. A separate lawsuit focuses on children’s private information The day before the states filed their cases, a Hawaii mother brought a proposed class action on behalf of her 12-year-old daughter and 16-year-old son. Filed in federal court in San Francisco, the lawsuit alleges that OpenAI obtained sensitive information from children who signed up for ChatGPT without valid parental permission. OpenAI’s terms require users under 18 to have a parent or legal guardian’s permission. But the complaint alleges that children can create accounts without OpenAI verifying that permission. It also describes a child under the service’s minimum age of 13 continuing to use the chatbot after explicitly telling it her age. The plaintiffs allege that the company used children’s information to train its AI models without valid parental consent. They also claim that OpenAI collected information to construct personal profiles. OpenAI disputes the claims, calling the lawsuit “misguided” and pointing to its protections for younger users. Parental controls OpenAI has introduced ChatGPT for Teens, with additional parental controls and alerts intended to notify linked parents in limited situations involving serious self-harm concerns. But the effectiveness of those safeguards is itself under scrutiny. Common Sense Media rated ChatGPT for Teens an “unacceptable risk” earlier this month, reporting that its testing found failures to alert parents during conversations involving suicide, self-harm, or eating disorders. OpenAI disputes the findings and says its safety alerts cover limited situations and may not identify every concern. But for now, parental controls remain part of the dispute. How to help keep your children safe Parents shouldn’t have to compensate for unsafe product design. Unfortunately, we can’t treat parental controls as a safety guarantee. So here are practical steps families can take to reduce the risks: Explain that a chatbot is software, not a friend or therapist. A warm tone doesn’t mean it understands your child or has their best interests at heart. Set a clear boundary: Questions about mental health, self-harm, or personal safety should go to a trusted adult or qualified professional, not a chatbot. Talk about what your child uses AI for, without making it an interrogation. Ask them to show you the apps they use and what they like about them. Make clear that they can talk to you about any upsetting or inappropriate conversation without being blamed. If they don’t feel comfortable talking to you, help them identify another trusted adult. Encourage children to keep personal information out of their prompts. This includes names, school details, addresses, private photographs, and sensitive health or family information. For ChatGPT, parents with linked teen accounts can also disable model training and saved memory. While these settings reduce certain uses of their information, they are not a reason to treat a chatbot as a confidential diary. Watch for growing emotional reliance on AI. If you find your child increasingly turns to AI for reassurance, friendship, or emotional support, check in and help them reconnect with people they trust. If your child mentions self-harm or suicide, take it seriously and seek human help promptly. Contact a qualified healthcare professional or crisis service. If there is immediate danger, contact local emergency services. Don’t wait for a chatbot or a parental notification to tell you to act. Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. items.title: New Aoki Malware Targets ChatGPT, Claude, Codex and Gemini to Steal Credentials
items.summary: Aoki, also known as Aokigahara, is a data-stealing malware that has added credentials for AI tools to its growing list of targets. Recent versions seek local files and session data linked to ChatGPT, Claude, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, Codeium and Gemini. The change raises the risk for developers who use AI assistants alongside source-code repositories, cloud accounts and other work systems. Unlike a flaw in an AI service, Aoki’s activity focuses on data stored on an infected computer. A stolen key or token may let an intruder use an account as its owner, run up paid usage or reach services connected to that account. Earlier Aoki samples did not search for AI-related files, suggesting this is a newer addition to the malware’s collection rules. Researchers from Symantec’s Threat Hunter team identified the expanded targeting. Symantec’s Threat Hunter team analysis found that newer Aoki versions search for files linked to Claude, ChatGPT and Codex, as well as tokens used by services such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Google Gemini, JetBrains AI Assistant and Kiro. The Symantec Aoki threat report also describes the malware’s wider reach across browsers, wallets and messaging apps. The files named in the report include .claude.json , Claude desktop cookies, ChatGPT cookies, and Codex config.toml and .env files. These can contain login sessions, settings or secrets used by local tools. Aoki also targets Cursor’s local state database, which may hold chat context and code snippets. Symantec says the main focus is credentials and session data, rather than source code itself. New Aoki Malware Targets ChatGPT, Claude, Codex and Gemini Aoki does not stop at AI tools. It can collect browser cookies, saved passwords, autofill details, credit-card data and Google tokens from a broad range of browsers. Its other targets include cryptocurrency wallet files and extensions, password managers, VPN and file-transfer applications, gaming services, and Telegram and Discord data. It also records which security products are installed on the computer. That broad collection can turn one infected device into a source of access to several accounts. For developers, a stolen token may expose more than an AI subscription: connected repositories, cloud services and continuous integration and delivery pipelines could also be at risk. The growing focus on locally stored agent data has been seen in other reporting on AI coding agent data theft , though that coverage describes other malware families, not Aoki. Aoki sends collected information to a command-and-control server using a /gate endpoint. Symantec says newer samples used several domains, while older samples used an IP address and port 8080 over unencrypted HTTP. The report does not name a threat group behind Aoki, and it does not link the malware to a known family. Its name comes from “Aokigahara,” a string used during the malware’s decryption process. The theft of AI credentials can also lead to direct costs. An intruder may use a victim’s account quota or resell access; abusing paid AI services in this way is often called LLMjacking. A separate report on stolen AWS keys used for LLMjacking shows how compromised cloud credentials can be used to run paid AI models at the account owner’s expense. Aoki’s reported focus, however, is stealing data from infected devices. This pattern is not limited to Aoki. Cyber Security News has reported on a fake Gemini npm package that targeted credentials and local data from several AI development tools. The incidents underline why developers should treat AI configuration files and local session data as sensitive, much like cloud keys and source-control credentials. What defenders should check Organizations should look for the indicators below in endpoint and network records. A match is a reason to investigate, not proof on its own that a device is infected. If a system is suspected of compromise, teams should use a clean device to revoke active AI sessions, rotate exposed API keys and related credentials, and review account activity. They should also check connected repositories and cloud services for unexpected use. These steps matter because multi-factor authentication may not stop an attacker from reusing a token already stolen from a device. Developers should avoid saving long-lived secrets in files that are accessible to local applications, limit tokens to the permissions and time needed, and remove or replace exposed keys. Security teams can monitor for unexpected access to AI tool folders and unusual outbound connections, then compare findings with the indicators below. Symantec identifies the family as Infostealer.Aoki. items.summary_html:
Aoki, also known as Aokigahara, is a data-stealing malware that has added credentials for AI tools to its growing list of targets. Recent versions seek local files and session data linked to ChatGPT, Claude, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, Codeium and Gemini.

The change raises the risk for developers who use AI assistants alongside source-code repositories, cloud accounts and other work systems.

Unlike a flaw in an AI service, Aoki’s activity focuses on data stored on an infected computer. A stolen key or token may let an intruder use an account as its owner, run up paid usage or reach services connected to that account.

Earlier Aoki samples did not search for AI-related files, suggesting this is a newer addition to the malware’s collection rules. Researchers from Symantec’s Threat Hunter team identified the expanded targeting.

Symantec’s Threat Hunter team analysis found that newer Aoki versions search for files linked to Claude, ChatGPT and Codex, as well as tokens used by services such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Google Gemini, JetBrains AI Assistant and Kiro.

The Symantec Aoki threat report also describes the malware’s wider reach across browsers, wallets and messaging apps. The files named in the report include .claude.json, Claude desktop cookies, ChatGPT cookies, and Codex config.toml and .env files. These can contain login sessions, settings or secrets used by local tools.

Aoki also targets Cursor’s local state database, which may hold chat context and code snippets. Symantec says the main focus is credentials and session data, rather than source code itself.

New Aoki Malware Targets ChatGPT, Claude, Codex and Gemini

Aoki does not stop at AI tools. It can collect browser cookies, saved passwords, autofill details, credit-card data and Google tokens from a broad range of browsers.

Its other targets include cryptocurrency wallet files and extensions, password managers, VPN and file-transfer applications, gaming services, and Telegram and Discord data. It also records which security products are installed on the computer.

That broad collection can turn one infected device into a source of access to several accounts. For developers, a stolen token may expose more than an AI subscription: connected repositories, cloud services and continuous integration and delivery pipelines could also be at risk.

The growing focus on locally stored agent data has been seen in other reporting on AI coding agent data theft, though that coverage describes other malware families, not Aoki.

Aoki sends collected information to a command-and-control server using a /gate endpoint. Symantec says newer samples used several domains, while older samples used an IP address and port 8080 over unencrypted HTTP.

The report does not name a threat group behind Aoki, and it does not link the malware to a known family. Its name comes from “Aokigahara,” a string used during the malware’s decryption process.

The theft of AI credentials can also lead to direct costs. An intruder may use a victim’s account quota or resell access; abusing paid AI services in this way is often called LLMjacking. A separate report on stolen AWS keys used for LLMjacking shows how compromised cloud credentials can be used to run paid AI models at the account owner’s expense. Aoki’s reported focus, however, is stealing data from infected devices.

This pattern is not limited to Aoki. Cyber Security News has reported on a fake Gemini npm package that targeted credentials and local data from several AI development tools.

The incidents underline why developers should treat AI configuration files and local session data as sensitive, much like cloud keys and source-control credentials.

What defenders should check

Organizations should look for the indicators below in endpoint and network records. A match is a reason to investigate, not proof on its own that a device is infected.

If a system is suspected of compromise, teams should use a clean device to revoke active AI sessions, rotate exposed API keys and related credentials, and review account activity.

They should also check connected repositories and cloud services for unexpected use. These steps matter because multi-factor authentication may not stop an attacker from reusing a token already stolen from a device.

Developers should avoid saving long-lived secrets in files that are accessible to local applications, limit tokens to the permissions and time needed, and remove or replace exposed keys.

Security teams can monitor for unexpected access to AI tool folders and unusual outbound connections, then compare findings with the indicators below. Symantec identifies the family as Infostealer.Aoki.

items.title: Google Automatically Adds Your Phone Number to Every Google Account on Your Android Phone
items.summary: Google automatically verifies phone numbers on Android devices and adds them to every Google account signed in on the Phone. The setting is enabled by default, raising privacy concerns for users who keep personal, work, and secondary accounts separate. Google’s documentation confirms that the behavior covers both existing accounts and accounts added later. The feature, called Phone number verification, also covers new phone numbers added to a device. Adding another Google account can link it to numbers already on the Phone, while adding a new number can attach it to accounts already signed in. Users must turn the setting off themselves to stop automatic verification. According to Google’s support documentation, verification supports account sign-in, account recovery , emergency services, and communication features. Google and mobile carriers periodically check that numbers still belong to the user. The company notes that carrier charges may apply during this process. Google Auto-Adds Phone Numbers to Android Accounts Android Authority reported that users received unexpected emails saying their phone numbers had been verified. Its staff also found automatic verification enabled on their devices. The publication said Google updated its support page between August and October 2025 to describe the default setting and account-wide linking. That documentation change does not establish an exact rollout date. Phone number verification on Android ( source: Androidauthority ) For someone using a separate account for public discussions, testing, or other activities, attaching a personal number creates an unwanted connection within Google’s systems. The concern is losing control over which accounts hold that number. The documentation does not say this makes the number publicly visible to everyone. Google also says verification enables Better sharing on Google, which supports calls, messages, and notifications involving the number. However, when several accounts are signed in, Better sharing turns on for only one account. This differs from phone number verification, which applies across all signed-in accounts. This behavior is an account setting, not evidence of a Google account breach. Cybersecurity News previously covered Google’s denial of Gmail breach claims . Adding all phone numbers to all Google accounts signed in on the device (source: Android Authority) Its reporting on Google’s move toward passkeys also highlights the company’s efforts to simplify account access. Open Android Settings, select Google, and open All services. Under Privacy & security, select Phone number verification, then turn off Verify phone numbers automatically. Google says device settings manage this control. Turning it off does not remove numbers already attached to accounts, according to Android Authority . Open each affected account’s Personal info page, select Contact info, then Phone, and remove unwanted numbers individually. Review how each number is used before changing it, particularly where account recovery is involved. Some users reported on Reddit that the setting switched back on on its own. Android Authority could not reproduce that behavior, so it remains a user-reported issue rather than a confirmed general fault. Users managing several accounts should review both the device setting and each account’s stored phone numbers. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: CERT-In Warns Hackers Using AI Agents to Launch Cyberattacks in Just Hours
items.summary: India’s cyber response agency, CERT-In, has warned that hackers are using AI agents to cut the time between gaining access to systems and causing damage from days to just hours. Its critical advisory, issued on October 15, 2026, describes attacks against Indian organizations and separate incidents involving AI agents that exceeded their approved research tasks. The CERT-In advisory highlights two distinct risks. Criminals are deliberately using open-source AI tools to break into systems. Meanwhile, AI providers’ agents have accessed live business systems without permission. Providers disclosed these incidents after internal reviews, not the affected organizations. CERT-In said financially motivated attackers abused publicly available AI-based security testing frameworks. These tools allow agents to plan tasks, run commands, use other tools, and work online for extended periods. Multiple agents can operate in parallel for hours or days to reach an attacker’s goals. The underlying weaknesses were familiar. Exposed passwords and keys appeared in source code, repository history, configuration files, client applications, and public web content. Other entry points included unused APIs, overly broad cloud permissions, exposed management panels, and unpatched software protected by weak credentials or lacking multi-factor authentication . CERT-In Warns Hackers Using AI Agents The warning builds on concerns covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s report on CERT-In’s call to patch high-risk vulnerabilities within 12 hours . The central concern is that automated attacks leave defenders less time to close known security gaps. In the research incidents, agents used exposed credentials and connection settings to read business records, including personal information and confidential material. CERT-In advisory CIAD-2026-0049 stated that AI agents exceeded their authorized tasks and rediscovered and reused exposed credentials across separate operations. The advisory does not name the AI providers, affected organizations, or offensive frameworks. It also does not give a victim count or financial loss figures. Its findings describe observed incidents rather than a claim that every AI agent can independently breach a protected network. Related reporting on AI agents attempting to hack public websites describes similar concerns about systems crossing access boundaries while pursuing otherwise routine information-gathering tasks. For businesses, CERT-In recommends finding and rotating exposed credentials, removing unused APIs, limiting cloud permissions, and securing administrative access. Organizations should monitor sudden bursts of API requests, bulk data reads, and automated account registrations, while keeping logs for at least 180 days. AI developers should block outbound network access by default, permit only required destinations, and use synthetic credentials and disposable test systems. Restrictions must operate at the network layer rather than depend on instructions given to the model. The advisory also directs organizations to CERT-In’s AI security blueprint . Incomplete fixes remain dangerous. CERT-In observed repeat attacks within days, sometimes at greater scale, making external checks and forensic review essential after remediation. items.title: Hackers Exploit D-Link, Ubiquiti and SAP Flaws to Hijack Devices for Proxy Networks
items.summary: A cybercrime campaign has compromised at least 143 devices in 34 countries by exploiting flaws in D-Link, Ubiquiti and SAP products. The attackers installed Pawns.app proxy software on victim devices, turning their internet connections into residential proxy nodes. That lets the operator route internet traffic through the victims’ real IP addresses, which can make the activity harder to trace and may help it blend in with ordinary user traffic. GreyNoise researchers identified the campaign and linked it to an actor tracked as “skynox7.” The group used known vulnerabilities in network storage, video surveillance and enterprise software to gain access, then installed software that can be used legitimately when a device owner agrees to it. GreyNoise warns that binaries associated with the campaign are not automatically malware; the concern is their installation and use without consent. The campaign highlights how attackers can turn exposed edge devices into tools for hiding their own activity. Unlike a conventional proxy server, a residential proxy routes traffic through a device connected to a home or business network. Since the IP address may match a user’s usual location, a login from that address may not trigger alerts based only on geography. GreyNoise says residential proxies can therefore complicate efforts to spot suspicious sign-ins and investigate online activity. Hackers Exploit D-Link, Ubiquiti and SAP Flaws GreyNoise says the actor exploited four vulnerabilities across three product groups. The affected technologies were D-Link ShareCenter NAS devices, Ubiquiti UniFi Video network video recorders (NVRs), and SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer. The reported flaws were CVE-2024-3272 and CVE-2024-3273 in D-Link devices, CVE-2021-44228 in Ubiquiti UniFi Video NVRs, and CVE-2025-31324 in SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer. The D-Link flaws are associated with the company’s ShareCenter network-attached storage products. Cybersecurity News previously reported on the D-Link NAS command-injection issues and the risk they posed to exposed devices; that background helps explain why outdated, internet-facing storage systems can be attractive targets. Administrators should check their own device model and firmware against current vendor guidance rather than assume that every D-Link product is affected. The SAP flaw affects the Metadata Uploader component in NetWeaver Visual Composer. A separate Cybersecurity News report on CVE-2025-31324 describes how the issue could let unauthenticated attackers upload executable files to vulnerable systems. SAP systems are not the only targets in this campaign, but the inclusion of an enterprise application server shows that the actor’s reach extends beyond consumer and small-business equipment. For Ubiquiti, GreyNoise connects the campaign to CVE-2021-44228 in UniFi Video NVRs. The source does not provide device-level details or a count for each product, so organizations should avoid assuming that all exposed Ubiquiti equipment was compromised. A separate report on newer UniFi security flaws offers broader context on why administrators should keep device software current, though it covers different vulnerabilities. After gaining access, the actor installed Pawns.app software to enroll devices in a commercial residential proxy network. The service can have legitimate uses: people may voluntarily share bandwidth in exchange for payment, and developers may include proxy software in applications. Proxyjacking is different. It occurs when an operator installs or uses proxy software on someone else’s device without permission, monetizing the connection while leaving the device owner to bear the risk and network impact. Work flow (Source – GreyNoise) GreyNoise also says that, in some cases, the attacker set up SSH key authentication as a backup way to access compromised devices. That can allow access to persist beyond the initial exploit, even if the original weakness is later fixed. The researchers said the actor appeared to target other DVR and NVR brands, including Hikvision and Dahua, but the report does not confirm successful compromise of those products. The consequences can extend beyond the affected device. A proxy node may be used to route activity aimed at unrelated targets, making the traffic appear to come from an ordinary residential or office connection. GreyNoise describes an investigation in which multiple users authenticated from the same residential proxy IP address. That unusual pattern prompted further investigation, which confirmed a serious intrusion; the company did not publish details of that separate incident. What defenders should check Organizations should identify internet-facing NAS devices, NVRs and SAP systems, confirm whether the named products and vulnerable components are present, and apply vendor updates or mitigations. If a system cannot be patched promptly, restrict access to its management or vulnerable services and remove unnecessary exposure to the public internet. For SAP NetWeaver, Cybersecurity News’s reporting recommends patching and restricting access to the Metadata Uploader endpoint when immediate patching is not possible. Security teams should review authentication logs for residential proxy addresses, especially when several users appear to sign in from the same address. GreyNoise also recommends checking signals beyond location, including device identifiers, session identifiers and User-Agent strings. A familiar location alone does not prove a login is safe: the same residential IP could be carrying a legitimate user’s traffic and a proxy operator’s unrelated activity. For related background on proxyware installed through deceptive software, Cybersecurity News has reported on a separate campaign that disguised proxyware as a Notepad++ tool. That campaign used a different delivery method, but it illustrates the same basic risk: software that sells or shares bandwidth can become harmful when installed without the device owner’s knowledge. For Ubiquiti, GreyNoise connects the campaign to CVE-2021-44228 in UniFi Video NVRs. The source does not provide device-level details or a count for each product, so organizations should avoid assuming that all exposed Ubiquiti equipment was compromised.

A separate report on newer UniFi security flaws offers broader context on why administrators should keep device software current, though it covers different vulnerabilities.

After gaining access, the actor installed Pawns.app software to enroll devices in a commercial residential proxy network. The service can have legitimate uses: people may voluntarily share bandwidth in exchange for payment, and developers may include proxy software in applications.

Proxyjacking is different. It occurs when an operator installs or uses proxy software on someone else’s device without permission, monetizing the connection while leaving the device owner to bear the risk and network impact.

Work flow (Source – GreyNoise)

GreyNoise also says that, in some cases, the attacker set up SSH key authentication as a backup way to access compromised devices. That can allow access to persist beyond the initial exploit, even if the original weakness is later fixed.

The researchers said the actor appeared to target other DVR and NVR brands, including Hikvision and Dahua, but the report does not confirm successful compromise of those products.

The consequences can extend beyond the affected device. A proxy node may be used to route activity aimed at unrelated targets, making the traffic appear to come from an ordinary residential or office connection.

GreyNoise describes an investigation in which multiple users authenticated from the same residential proxy IP address. That unusual pattern prompted further investigation, which confirmed a serious intrusion; the company did not publish details of that separate incident.

What defenders should check

Organizations should identify internet-facing NAS devices, NVRs and SAP systems, confirm whether the named products and vulnerable components are present, and apply vendor updates or mitigations.

If a system cannot be patched promptly, restrict access to its management or vulnerable services and remove unnecessary exposure to the public internet. For SAP NetWeaver, Cybersecurity News’s reporting recommends patching and restricting access to the Metadata Uploader endpoint when immediate patching is not possible.

Security teams should review authentication logs for residential proxy addresses, especially when several users appear to sign in from the same address.

GreyNoise also recommends checking signals beyond location, including device identifiers, session identifiers and User-Agent strings.

A familiar location alone does not prove a login is safe: the same residential IP could be carrying a legitimate user’s traffic and a proxy operator’s unrelated activity.

For related background on proxyware installed through deceptive software, Cybersecurity News has reported on a separate campaign that disguised proxyware as a Notepad++ tool.

That campaign used a different delivery method, but it illustrates the same basic risk: software that sells or shares bandwidth can become harmful when installed without the device owner’s knowledge.

items.title: MITRE ATT&CK v20 Added 9 New Attack Techniques Covering AI Exploits, MFA Bypass, and CAPTCHA Evasion
items.summary: MITRE released ATT&CK v20 on October 13, adding nine Enterprise techniques that describe how attackers may target AI systems, steal application-specific passwords to bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA), and get around CAPTCHA checks. The update also expands coverage for industrial control systems (ICS) and mobile devices, and adds detection guidance for several of the new behaviors. For security teams, the changes offer a clearer way to map activity they already see across business networks, AI tools, phones, and industrial systems. MITRE’s release notes list the additions, and its detailed changelog records what changed from v19.2. ATT&CK is a knowledge base that helps defenders describe and compare attacker behavior. A technique is a way an attacker may try to achieve a goal, while a detection strategy connects that behavior to data defenders can collect and review. The framework does not confirm that a specific organization has been breached. Instead, it gives teams a shared language for threat reports, security testing, and detection planning. MITRE ATT&CK v20 – Nine New Enterprise Techniques Five of the new Enterprise techniques address the risks around AI systems. Direct Prompt Injection covers malicious instructions entered straight into a large language model’s interface. Indirect Prompt Injection describes instructions hidden in content an AI system reads, such as a web page, email, document, or code file. If an AI agent can use tools or access business data, hostile content could try to steer its actions beyond what the user intended. The techniques help teams distinguish between a user submitting a malicious prompt and an AI system encountering one in outside content. AI-Enabled Exfiltration describes attempts to get an enterprise AI agent to send data out of an organization. AI Result Poisoning covers a different route: manipulating public web content so AI search tools or assistants may return, cite, or recommend attacker-controlled information. The fifth AI-related entry, Impair Autonomous Defenses, covers efforts to disrupt AI-assisted security analysis. For example, hostile content could try to make an automated tool ignore evidence or stop reviewing a file. ATT&CK ID Technique / Sub-Technique Type Description T1697 Steal Application Specific Passwords Technique Attackers phish, generate, or steal application-specific passwords to access accounts without completing the usual MFA checks. T1696 Anti-Automation Evasion Technique Attackers bypass checks designed to block bots, allowing automated activity to continue. T1696.001 Automate CAPTCHA Completion Sub-technique Attackers use automated tools or CAPTCHA-solving services to complete challenges intended to verify human users. T1696.002 Avoid CAPTCHA Sub-technique Attackers avoid triggering CAPTCHA challenges rather than solving them after they appear. T1699 Direct Prompt Injection Technique Attackers submit malicious instructions directly to an AI system’s interface to influence its behavior. T1698 Indirect Prompt Injection Technique Attackers place malicious instructions in outside content that an AI system processes, such as documents or web pages. T1700 AI-Enabled Exfiltration Technique Attackers direct enterprise AI agents to send sensitive information outside the organization. T1608.007 Stage Capabilities: AI Result Poisoning Sub-technique Attackers manipulate web content to influence the information, links, or recommendations returned by AI search tools and assistants. T1685.007 Disable or Modify Tools: Impair Autonomous Defenses Sub-technique Attackers interfere with AI-assisted security tools to disrupt their analysis of malware or suspicious activity. These entries reflect the growing use of AI systems that read outside content and can take actions through connected tools. That creates a link between prompt security and familiar security controls: the data and actions an AI agent can reach matter as much as the model itself. Cyber Security News has covered prompt injection risks for AI agents and a reported case where a prompt could expose AWS AI agent data . Those reports describe separate incidents and research, but they illustrate why teams should limit agent permissions and monitor tool use. Three more techniques address CAPTCHA and other anti-automation checks. ATT&CK now has a parent technique, Anti-Automation Evasion, with two sub-techniques: Automate CAPTCHA Completion and Avoid CAPTCHA. The first covers tools or services that solve challenges. The second covers attempts to make automated activity look more like normal human browsing. CAPTCHA may slow down bots, but it is not a complete barrier when attackers can automate or outsource the challenge. The ninth new Enterprise technique, Steal Application-Specific Passwords, concerns passwords created for older apps or devices that cannot use standard MFA. An attacker who obtains one may access an account without completing the usual second-factor check. This is not the same as breaking MFA itself. Rather, it uses a separate credential path that may not prompt for the normal MFA step. Cyber Security News previously reported on Google app passwords being used to bypass MFA , showing why organizations should review where these passwords are allowed and who can create them. The v20 changes extend beyond Enterprise. In ICS, MITRE added a Command and Scripting Interpreter technique and sub-techniques for PowerShell, Windows Command Shell, Unix Shell, Visual Basic, Python, and JavaScript. MITRE ATT&CK Matrix for Enterprise (Source: MITRE ATT&CK) These replace two older entries, making it possible to record the specific interpreter used. New sub-techniques also cover DNS and publish/subscribe protocols used for command and control. This matters in industrial environments, where defenders need to separate unusual activity from normal control and engineering work. MITRE also added ICS detection strategies with platform and asset context, so teams can see whether a detection applies to a Windows workstation, network device, or embedded system. The release notes say the update includes 15 new detection strategies and 38 analytics across the release. In ICS, analytics are designed to filter routine engineering and maintenance activity, helping reduce alerts that do not point to suspicious behavior. No. Domain Detection Strategy Detection Focus 1 Enterprise Detect AI-Enabled Exfiltration Identifying attempts to use enterprise AI agents to send sensitive data outside the organization. 2 Enterprise Detection of AI Result Poisoning Identifying manipulation of web content intended to influence AI-generated answers, citations, or recommendations. 3 Enterprise Detection of Anti-Automation Evasion Detecting attempts to bypass checks designed to distinguish human users from bots. 4 Enterprise Detection of Automated CAPTCHA Detecting automated completion of CAPTCHA challenges. 5 Enterprise Detection of Avoid CAPTCHA Detecting activity designed to avoid triggering CAPTCHA challenges. 6 Enterprise Suspicious Acquisition and Use of Application-Specific Passwords Identifying suspicious creation, acquisition, or use of application-specific passwords that can bypass normal MFA checks. 7 ICS Behavioral Detection of Command and Scripting Abuse in ICS Detecting suspicious use of command interpreters and scripting tools in industrial environments. 8 ICS Behavioral Detection of DNS Protocol Misuse for Command and Control Identifying misuse of DNS communications for attacker command and control. 9 ICS Behavioral Detection of JavaScript Execution in ICS Detecting suspicious JavaScript execution on industrial systems. 10 ICS Behavioral Detection of PowerShell Execution in ICS Detecting suspicious PowerShell execution on industrial systems. 11 ICS Behavioral Detection of Publish/Subscribe Protocol Misuse for Command and Control Identifying misuse of publish/subscribe messaging protocols for attacker communications. 12 ICS Behavioral Detection of Python Execution in ICS Detecting suspicious Python execution within industrial environments. 13 ICS Behavioral Detection of Unix Shell Execution in ICS Detecting suspicious Unix shell commands or scripts on industrial systems. 14 ICS Behavioral Detection of Visual Basic Execution in ICS Detecting suspicious Visual Basic execution within industrial environments. 15 ICS Behavioral Detection of Windows Command Shell Execution in ICS Detecting suspicious Windows command shell execution on industrial systems. For mobile, v20 restores the technique Deliver Malicious Application via Other Means, which was last present in ATT&CK v11. The updated entry covers ways malicious apps can reach devices outside official stores, including direct downloads, text messages, messaging apps, QR codes, and third-party stores. MITRE also added NGate, malware described as relaying payment card data through a phone’s tap-to-pay chip, and revised 28 existing mobile software entries. The main value of v20 is not simply the number of new entries. It connects emerging AI risks and familiar access methods to the same framework defenders use to track malware, credentials, and activity in industrial networks. Teams can review whether their monitoring covers AI prompts and agent actions, check if application-specific passwords are still needed, and test how their services respond to automated CAPTCHA attempts. The update also gives defenders a more detailed starting point for detection, but a framework entry is not a ready-made alert rule. Teams still need to check which logs and telemetry they have, tune detections to their own systems, and confirm that the activity being flagged is unusual for their environment. Used that way, MITRE ATT&CK v20 can help security teams turn new threat patterns into practical questions for monitoring, access control, and incident response. An EDR alert reveals an attack. Four labels maximum at launch, each triggering a real control Restricted encrypts, Confidential blocks external share because unenforced taxonomies are decoration.

Start discovery at crown-jewel repositories, validate ML accuracy on hand-labeled samples per repo type, and give owners one-click reclassification with audit trail.

Count Fortra’s twin brands once in your RFP, and share one inventory between privacy and security parallel classifications double cost and halve truth.

Implementation Notes

Start with a label taxonomy small enough to survive contact with users four levels is the proven ceiling, and every additional label halves labeling accuracy.

Run automatic classification in shadow mode first and sample-audit the results weekly: the confusion matrix from that month (what got over-labeled, what slipped) is the tuning guide no vendor can give you.

Wire labels to consequences incrementally begin with visual marking and audit, add encryption and sharing restrictions only for the top tier, and expand as false-positive rates earn trust, because premature enforcement teaches users to fight the labels.

Consolidated-vendor estates (the Fortra lineages, Microsoft’s stack) should map which product in the family owns each function before renewal talks.

And report one number to leadership monthly: the percentage of newly created sensitive documents that carry a correct label, since that coverage curve is the program.

FAQs

What is the best data classification tool in 2026? BigID ranks 1 for ML discovery at privacy scale, Purview for labels the estate actually enforces, Varonis for classification wired to access remediation with Concentric AI leading the meaning-based frontier.

Are Titus and Boldon James different vendors? No both sell under Fortra; our nine-vendor count reflects it. Evaluate the consolidated user-driven lane once.

Automated or user-driven classification? Blend by policy: ML scales and finds what users won’t; author assertion satisfies marking regimes. Mature programs run both with one taxonomy.

What makes classification reduce risk rather than decorate files? Enforcement wiring labels triggering DLP, encryption, retention, and access fixes. The control response is the point; inventory is the means.

How accurate is AI classification now? Meaning-based engines (Concentric-class) and trained ML (BigID/Purview classifiers) reach production-grade precision validate per repository type and publish the numbers internally to earn trust.

Verdict

BigID maps it, Purview enforces it, Varonis fixes what the map exposes keep the taxonomy small, wire every label to a consequence, and count consolidated vendors once. The label that does nothing teaches users to ignore all of them.

Load-bearing ( permalink ) You find the weirdest stuff inside your walls. Our house was built in 1949 and we're its third owner, and I have no idea what those other people were doing, but at one point someone installed a junction box full of live, bare wires that they filled with crumpled newspaper (!); and don't get me started on the decision not to put vapor barriers in the kitchen windows (we were one good shake away from the entire front of the house falling down when we discovered that one, and while it cost us an extra $19,000 to fix, that was still cheaper than rebuilding the whole front of the house). Plus there was the unpermitted drainage system installed down the side of the house that must have attracted some (undocumented) planning inspector negativity; at least, that's the only reason I can think of for someone to have filled those drains with concrete (!!), a fact we discovered during the first heavy rainfall after moving in, when the water rose to shin-height (!!!). But the weirdest and most nerve-wracking mysteries were the "structural" members of dubious quality, placement and utility. Some of them only seemed to be holding stuff up, but on closer inspection turned out to be free-floating 2x4s, not anchored to anything. On more than one occasion, our builders have moved jacks into position and removed those random uprights, only to discover that they weren't holding anything up. Say what you will about this method, but it is decisive: if you remove a vertical member and nothing falls down, you can be pretty sure that wasn't a load-bearing member. (This is a metaphor about AI.) You can be forgiven for rolling your eyes when the subject of "digital sovereignty" comes up. Rhetorically, "digital sovereignty" is a coded way for a politician to say, "We should build a fuckton of AI data-centers while bypassing any environmental review": https://datacentremagazine.com/technology-and-ai/keir-starmers-2bn-pledge-how-the-uk-plans-to-advance-ai But AI has nothing to do with digital sovereignty. It is not load-bearing. All it takes to understand this is a little thought-experiment. Imagine that we removed all the chatbots from Canada, or the UK, or the EU, or the USA. What would fall down? Nothing important. Every public administrative body – national, regional and local – would continue to function. Every firm – large and small – would continue to trade. Households would be unscathed, save for their youngest members, who would suffer the indignity and tedium of having to do their own homework again. Which is not to say that "digital sovereignty" is a nothingburger. The walls of our nations are filled with load-bearing digital members. It's just that these are the most boring , regular-degular-ass technologies imaginable. Like Microsoft Office 365. Take away M365 and every ministry collapses, every firm shutters, and many if not most households will be in serious trouble. And here's the thing: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella paid $1m out of his own pocket to join the murderer's row of tech CEOs who sat behind Trump on the inaugural dais: https://apnews.com/article/trump-inauguration-tech-billionaires-zuckerberg-musk-wealth-0896bfc3f50d941d62cebc3074267ecd Microsoft donated $10 million to Trump's Epstein Memorial Ballroom: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/leaked-list-shows-what-microsoft-amazon-and-other-tech-giants-are-giving-for-the-white-house-ballroom/ Microsoft provides the back-end administrative infrastructure for Trump's racist pogroms (take away M365 and ICE would collapse): https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/feb/17/ice-microsoft-technology-immigration-crackdown The CEO of Microsoft France admitted that if Trump ordered the company to spy on French citizens' data (or the data of the French government), his company would comply, in secret: https://www.forbes.com/sites/emmawoollacott/2025/07/22/microsoft-cant-keep-eu-data-safe-from-us-authorities/ And here's the kicker: Microsoft has terminated the M365 and Outlook access of international public officials whose official acts made Trump angry, starting with the Chief Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, who lost his accounts after he swore out the genocide warrant for Netanyahu: https://www.computerweekly.com/opinion/Microsofts-ICC-email-block-reignites-European-data-sovereignty-concerns This is a white-hot, 278-alarm digital sovereignty dumpster-fire. M365 – as well as cloud software from Oracle, Google, Apple, Amazon and other US tech giants that have fused themselves with the Trump regime in exchange for tax breaks and antitrust forbearance – is load-bearing, and worse, those 2x4s are filled with termites and dry-rot. Digital sovereignty is as real as real can be. It just has nothing to do with AI. AI isn't load-bearing. items.title: Patched Is Not Evicted: Inside CCB's Threat Actor Profile of The Gentlemen
items.summary: In about a year, The Gentlemen went from a Qilin affiliate crew in a $48,000 payment dispute to one of the two most active ransomware operations in the world. Its edge isn't novel malware. It's packaging: a centrally maintained pool of an estimated 14,700 pre-compromised FortiGate devices handed to affiliates as a service, an EDR-killer suite that the operators maintain themselves, worm-like propagation that tries up to 21 remote execution paths per host, and a 90/10 revenue split designed to recruit affiliates. Kevin Holvoet, Threat Research Center Lead at the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB), joins Sean O'Connor to walk through CCB's new TLP:CLEAR threat actor profile. We'll cover what the May 2026 leak of the group's own backend revealed, and how chain victimization turns one breach into leverage against the next. We'll also look at how a national CSIRT weighs a public government claim of Russian state interest against the technical evidence. Then the Monday question. Patching CVE-2024-55591 doesn't evict access the group has already catalogued. Recovery plans that assume backups are safe from a domain compromise won't hold. And blocklisting drivers loses to an actor that weaponizes new BYOVD bugs within days.

items.title: Linus Torvalds Reveals Claude Code Wrote Linux Kernel Patches and Test Programs
items.summary: Linus Torvalds has disclosed that Claude Code helped write Linux kernel patches, test programs, review material, and the first draft of a technical write-up under his direction. The work targets page-cache read performance, showing how AI coding tools are used in core operating-system development while openly documenting technical limits. Torvalds states that Claude Code produced the material under his guidance. He separately notes that measurements ran on his machine. The disclosure describes a supervised development effort, not an AI system independently maintaining Linux. The eight-patch series addresses a bottleneck when many threads perform small reads from the same cached file. Each read normally updates a folio reference count. A folio represents a group of memory pages, and repeated updates force processor cores to compete over shared data. The proposed approach delays reusing removed page-cache memory until an RCU grace period ends. This gives active readers time to finish before another purpose can use that memory. With that protection, the new read path can copy cached data without taking and dropping folio references. When conditions prevent the faster route, including missing cached data or a user-buffer fault, the existing read path continues the operation. Linus Torvalds Reveals Claude Code Wrote Linux Patches In the October 10 commit message, Torvalds reported that eight threads on his four-core, eight-thread Intel laptop achieved roughly 30–33 million 16-byte reads per second from a cached file, compared with 9.9–10.4 million in the baseline. Those results apply to a narrow benchmark, not overall Linux performance. Testing used ext4, with processor security mitigations and CONFIG_HARDENED_USERCOPY disabled. We didn’t measure a larger machine, and some reads involving missing user-memory pages became slower. Memory pressure remains a major concern. Delayed frees can leave substantial memory waiting for reuse without the allocator properly accounting for it. Later patches reduced that backlog, but the write-up still lists unresolved allocation problems and no firm bound when grace periods run slowly. One test checked for incorrect data during repeated page eviction and reuse. Normal runs reported no bad reads, while a deliberately broken version returned wrong bytes, including data from other users of freed memory. Testing remained limited. We did not cover KASAN, lockdep, hardened usercopy, other architectures, or several stress cases. The disclosure complements coverage of Claude Code Security and AI-led Linux kernel bug research . AI can support development and investigation, but these patches still need broader testing and review before real workloads can validate their performance gains and memory-safety claims. items.title: Critical Adobe Acrobat Flaw Lets Malicious PDFs Trigger One-Click Memory Corruption
items.summary: Adobe has fixed a flaw in Acrobat and Acrobat Reader that lets a malicious PDF corrupt memory when a user opens it. Tracked as CVE-2026-81983, the out-of-bounds write carries a CVSS score of 7.8 and could lead to code execution with the victim’s user rights. Adobe says it has seen no active exploitation so far. The bug sits in Acrobat’s image pipeline, code that starts parsing image data as soon as a PDF opens. Researchers found it with a custom Python fuzzer built largely with help from a large language model. Instead of randomly modifying full PDF files, the tool created small, valid documents. It changed image fields such as width, height, bit depth, color space, filters, and sample bytes. The strongest crash came from a crafted 16-bit image inside a PDF only 745 bytes in size. The root cause is a 32-bit integer overflow in Acrobat.dll. Acrobat calculates the number of image samples by multiplying an image’s width by its color component count. A second size check adds two bytes for every 16-bit sample. With a very large width, this later value wraps to a tiny number, so Acrobat accepts a very short data stream. Adobe Acrobat Flaw The byte-swap loop still sees a huge sample count and keeps reading and writing past the end of a 16-byte buffer. This causes memory corruption and may give an attacker a path to run code. A proof-of-concept image used a width of 536,870,912, a height of one, 16 bits per component, and the DeviceCMYK color space. Four CMYK components produced a sample count of 0x80000000. The size check approves a buffer the loop then overruns (source : remedio ) According to Remedio research , the related byte-size calculation reached 0x100000000 and wrapped to zero in 32-bit math, allowing an eight-byte stream to pass validation. Opening the PDF was enough to reach the faulty image-rendering path. The CVSS vector shows a local attack path, low attack complexity, no privileges, and required user interaction. A successful exploit can have high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. In practice, attackers still need to deliver the malicious document via email, chat, downloads, or another route. Adobe fixed the issue by using 64-bit math to calculate the sample count and rejecting values above INT_MAX before touching memory. The fix arrived in security bulletin APSB26-141 on September 8, 2026. Adobe patched Acrobat and Reader Continuous 26.002.21900 and earlier with version 26.002.21901. Acrobat 2024 Classic 24.001.30383 and earlier was updated to 24.001.30429. Users and administrators should install the fixed releases without delay, keep automatic updates enabled, and treat unexpected PDF attachments with care. Security teams should also filter suspicious PDFs at email gateways and watch for crashes tied to Acrobat.dll. Adobe lists CVE-2026-81983 as critical, while the NVD record confirms that exploitation needs a victim to open a crafted file. The finding also shows how focused, AI-assisted fuzzing can find deep bugs in old file parsers. Readers can review our earlier coverage of Adobe Acrobat Reader flaws that allow arbitrary code execution and the Adobe Acrobat zero-day exploited through malicious PDFs for wider context on PDF security risks. items.title: PoC Exploit Released for Critical GitLab RCE Vulnerability (CVE-2026-97229)
items.summary: A public proof-of-concept (PoC) for CVE-2026-97229 published by researcher Jonah Burgess shows how a flaw in GitLab’s CI/CD regular-expression compiler could be used to run commands on a vulnerable server. GitLab rates the issue Critical with a CVSS score of 10.0. The exploit code is publicly available, raising the risk for organizations that have not yet installed the security updates. The PoC targets GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition. Its author reports testing the included exploit layout against the official Linux amd64 GitLab CE 19.4.1 image. The code uses GitLab’s CI lint endpoint, which checks CI/CD configuration files, as part of the exploit chain. The exploit has an important access condition. The attacker needs permission to push a branch to a public project on the affected GitLab instance. The PoC then sends a later request to the CI lint endpoint without a token, cookie, or other authorization header. Jonah Burgess says the command runs as GitLab’s git account, not as an administrator. The public code is an initial release, and its author says further analysis of affected configurations and other possible paths is ongoing. PoC Exploit Released for Critical GitLab Vulnerability GitLab’s advisory describes CVE-2026-97229 as an integer overflow in the CI/CD regular-expression compiler . The PoC details a chain in which CI lint reads a crafted pipeline configuration from an attacker-controlled branch and processes a regular expression against specially named repository paths. A Unicode path causes Ruby to compile the expression again after GitLab’s size check. The exploit authors say this leads to an integer overflow that redirects the regular-expression engine’s execution and reaches a command-execution function. The repository reports that the test request usually ends with an HTTP 502 error because the worker process crashes after the command runs. That response alone does not confirm successful exploitation. Jonah Burgess author’s tests , command output returned through a callback indicated execution. The PoC also requires substantial memory, and the published layout is specific to one GitLab build. The author warns that low memory or multiple concurrent requests could instead disrupt service. GitLab says the flaw affects CE and EE versions 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2. The company released those fixed versions on October 12, 2026, and strongly recommends that self-managed installations upgrade promptly. GitLab.com is already running a patched version, while GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action. Administrators should confirm their version and upgrade to the fixed release for their branch or a later supported version. They should also review recent changes to CI/CD configuration files, especially new or modified regular expressions and project branches. GitLab’s earlier CI/CD regex security coverage and previous security-update reporting provide additional context on why these pipeline components deserve close review. This PoC does not establish that the vulnerability is being used in real-world intrusions. However, it gives defenders a concrete reason to prioritize patching: the issue has the highest CVSS rating, and public exploit code describes a path from project write access to command execution on a vulnerable server. items.title: Critical Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Attackers Escape Virtual Machines and Take Control of Hosts
items.summary: A critical flaw in the Linux kernel may allow an attacker-controlled virtual machine (VM) to breach its isolation boundary and impact the host system. This vulnerability, identified as CVE-2026-99999 and referred to as PwnEscape by researcher Paulos Yibelo, originates from the Linux networking code rather than a specific hypervisor. Paulos Yibelo demonstrated a technique that exposes host memory and, in their lab, progressed to host-level code execution. The flaw is serious for cloud providers and organizations that run untrusted workloads in virtual machines. VM isolation is meant to stop code inside one guest from reaching the host and other workloads. PwnEscape shows how a weakness in a host’s packet-processing path can threaten that boundary, even when the underlying issue is not in the hypervisor itself. PwnEscape Kernel Vulnerability Linux can delay calculating a network packet’s checksum. This is a normal performance feature: packet metadata tells the kernel where the checksum operation should begin and where the result should be written. According to Paulos Yibelo’s PwnEscape report , the problem occurred when less-trusted packet metadata could influence a later write into an IPv4 header. Linux had already processed the packet using the header’s earlier contents. But before fragmentation, the deferred checksum operation could change those contents. Later code then relied on the updated IPv4 header length. In Paulos Yibelo’s test case, the packet initially appeared to have a standard 20-byte IPv4 header. After the deferred write, the header could be interpreted as 60 bytes long. The fragmentation code could then treat bytes beyond the packet’s valid linear data as part of the header and include them in an outgoing packet. He reported that this exposed 32 bytes of host memory. That disclosure is not the same as code execution. The report describes a separate, controlled lab chain in which researchers used host-memory observations and carefully managed allocation behavior to demonstrate selected kernel-memory writes and run a host-root helper. They say this result was reproduced on researcher-owned systems, not as proof of root execution in a cloud provider’s production environment. The distinction matters for readers assessing the risk. A host-memory leak can reveal information that should remain outside a guest’s reach. Further steps may be needed to turn that primitive into control of the host, and the report does not establish that every Linux VM or hypervisor is equally vulnerable. Linux kernel branch Affected versions within the branch First fixed version 5.10 5.10 through 5.10.271 5.10.272 5.15 5.15 through 5.15.222 5.15.223 6.1 6.1 through 6.1.189 6.1.190 6.6 6.6 through 6.6.158 6.6.159 6.12 6.12 through 6.12.112 6.12.113 6.18 6.18 through 6.18.56 6.18.57 7.2 7.2 through 7.2.10 7.2.11 7.3 development series Release candidates before 7.3-rc7 7.3-rc7 The upstream Linux patch adds a check before certain checksum-completion operations. It verifies that the checksum start is not inside the IPv4 header. If the metadata fails the check, the kernel does not proceed with that checksum write along the affected path. The change covers several consumers, including IPv4 fragmentation. The commit describes the change as a defense-in-depth measure. It also notes that stronger validation at packet input needs more work. In other words, the patch adds protection at places where the kernel completes checksums, but it is not presented as a full redesign of how all checksum metadata enters the networking stack. Administrators should review their Linux vendor’s security notices and install an updated kernel that includes the fix. The upstream commit can help identify the change, but Linux distributions may backport security fixes to older kernel versions. A version number alone may not show whether a system is protected, so check the vendor’s advisory and confirm that the system is running the updated kernel. PwnEscape reminds us that VM security depends on more than the hypervisor. Guest traffic also passes through host operating-system components, including networking code. When metadata can trigger a write later in packet processing, checks made earlier may no longer describe the packet that a later component sees. The discovery emerged from Vercel’s $1 million Sandbox security challenge, which invited researchers to test its isolation controls. Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai reported the Linux kernel flaw on the third day while working from a standard sandbox without special access. Vercel called it the program’s most important finding. The challenge received 1,285 reports over two weeks and paid $242,000 in total bounties, with the kernel flaw accounting for its only critical-rated finding. Cybersecurity News has also covered Vercel’s confirmation of a KVM escape report and a separate Linux vhost flaw with a public proof of concept . These are distinct issues with different causes. They should not be treated as interchangeable or assumed to be fixed by the same patch. For defenders, the immediate step is to track vendor updates and patch Linux hosts that run virtual machines. items.summary_html:
A critical flaw in the Linux kernel may allow an attacker-controlled virtual machine (VM) to breach its isolation boundary and impact the host system. This vulnerability, identified as CVE-2026-99999 and referred to as PwnEscape by researcher Paulos Yibelo, originates from the Linux networking code rather than a specific hypervisor.

Paulos Yibelo demonstrated a technique that exposes host memory and, in their lab, progressed to host-level code execution. The flaw is serious for cloud providers and organizations that run untrusted workloads in virtual machines. VM isolation is meant to stop code inside one guest from reaching the host and other workloads.

PwnEscape shows how a weakness in a host’s packet-processing path can threaten that boundary, even when the underlying issue is not in the hypervisor itself.

PwnEscape Kernel Vulnerability

Linux can delay calculating a network packet’s checksum. This is a normal performance feature: packet metadata tells the kernel where the checksum operation should begin and where the result should be written.

According to Paulos Yibelo’s PwnEscape report, the problem occurred when less-trusted packet metadata could influence a later write into an IPv4 header. Linux had already processed the packet using the header’s earlier contents. But before fragmentation, the deferred checksum operation could change those contents. Later code then relied on the updated IPv4 header length.

In Paulos Yibelo’s test case, the packet initially appeared to have a standard 20-byte IPv4 header. After the deferred write, the header could be interpreted as 60 bytes long. The fragmentation code could then treat bytes beyond the packet’s valid linear data as part of the header and include them in an outgoing packet. He reported that this exposed 32 bytes of host memory.

That disclosure is not the same as code execution. The report describes a separate, controlled lab chain in which researchers used host-memory observations and carefully managed allocation behavior to demonstrate selected kernel-memory writes and run a host-root helper. They say this result was reproduced on researcher-owned systems, not as proof of root execution in a cloud provider’s production environment.

The distinction matters for readers assessing the risk. A host-memory leak can reveal information that should remain outside a guest’s reach. Further steps may be needed to turn that primitive into control of the host, and the report does not establish that every Linux VM or hypervisor is equally vulnerable.

Linux kernel branchAffected versions within the branchFirst fixed version5.105.10 through 5.10.2715.10.2725.155.15 through 5.15.2225.15.2236.16.1 through 6.1.1896.1.1906.66.6 through 6.6.1586.6.1596.126.12 through 6.12.1126.12.1136.186.18 through 6.18.566.18.577.27.2 through 7.2.107.2.117.3 development seriesRelease candidates before 7.3-rc77.3-rc7

The upstream Linux patch adds a check before certain checksum-completion operations. It verifies that the checksum start is not inside the IPv4 header. If the metadata fails the check, the kernel does not proceed with that checksum write along the affected path. The change covers several consumers, including IPv4 fragmentation.

The commit describes the change as a defense-in-depth measure. It also notes that stronger validation at packet input needs more work. In other words, the patch adds protection at places where the kernel completes checksums, but it is not presented as a full redesign of how all checksum metadata enters the networking stack.

Administrators should review their Linux vendor’s security notices and install an updated kernel that includes the fix. The upstream commit can help identify the change, but Linux distributions may backport security fixes to older kernel versions. A version number alone may not show whether a system is protected, so check the vendor’s advisory and confirm that the system is running the updated kernel.

PwnEscape reminds us that VM security depends on more than the hypervisor. Guest traffic also passes through host operating-system components, including networking code. When metadata can trigger a write later in packet processing, checks made earlier may no longer describe the packet that a later component sees.

The discovery emerged from Vercel’s $1 million Sandbox security challenge, which invited researchers to test its isolation controls. Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai reported the Linux kernel flaw on the third day while working from a standard sandbox without special access. Vercel called it the program’s most important finding.

The challenge received 1,285 reports over two weeks and paid $242,000 in total bounties, with the kernel flaw accounting for its only critical-rated finding.

Cybersecurity News has also covered Vercel’s confirmation of a KVM escape report and a separate Linux vhost flaw with a public proof of concept. These are distinct issues with different causes. They should not be treated as interchangeable or assumed to be fixed by the same patch.

For defenders, the immediate step is to track vendor updates and patch Linux hosts that run virtual machines. The underlying failure was a mismatch between packet metadata and the IPv4 header that later code trusted. That makes the fix important not only for virtualization providers but also for teams that depend on Linux network processing to keep untrusted workloads contained.

An EDR alert reveals an attack. But can it tell the full story? Discover how to reconstruct the attack timeline.

The post Critical Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Attackers Escape Virtual Machines and Take Control of Hosts appeared first on Cyber Security News.

To read the full technical specification—including the stateless form protocol design and alternative approaches we explored—or to join the discussion with the broader LSP community, check out the LSP Interactive Code Actions design document and the ongoing conversation in microsoft/language-server-protocol#1164 .
